div.p: Translocation programs are used in species conservation, but their success rates, particularly in Australia, are low. The poor outcomes for translocation programs are commonly attributed to a lack of information about habitat requirements, especially for rare and endangered species. To address this, the identification of suitable release sites using analytical methods such as Habitat Suitability Models (HSM), has become common. Since biodiversity losses are predicted to increase in the future, effective strategies to reduce species decline are required. Evidence-based decisions and scientific data to support conservation decision-making is paramount in conservation efforts.

Once widely distributed across the mountainous country of south-eastern Australia, the distribution of the Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (BTRW) has contracted particularly within the southern extent of their range. Considered critically endangered in Victoria and extinct in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT), it is more important than ever that the habitat requirements of the BTRW are understood to inform future translocations and the protection of this species in the wild.

In this study, an explicit decision-making process was combined with Habitat Suitability Modelling (HSM) and ground-truthing methods to inform potential Brush-tailed Rockwallaby (BTRW) translocations sites within Victoria and the ACT.
iii Although this study is not the first of its kind to use HSM to predict BTRW habitat suitability, it is the first of its kind to apply an explicit decision-making process at two key stages:

1. to inform the selection of key physical and management attributes to be used in a HSM; and 2. to prioritise sites, within experts' local knowledge areas, for ground-truthing By combining HSM and an explicit decision-making process, this study has been able to identify six suitable and two highly suitable habitat for BTRW across Victoria and the ACT. The use of an explicit decision-making process and ground-truthing methods to validate the model outputs and prioritise sites for ground-truthing has ensured that the final ranking of potential candidate sites can be reliably used by the Southern Brushtailed Rock-wallaby Recovery Team to inform future translocations.

• Use a panel of experts and a Structured Decision Making (SDM) approach (Gregory et al. 2012) to evaluate the importance of each habitat variable in determining habitat suitability for new BTRW colonies. • Use a panel of experts and a Structured Decision Making (SDM) approach (Gregory et al. 2012) to rank the candidate sites in order of priority for consideration as potential release sites for captive bred BTRW individuals. Despite significant advances in conservation management, the total number of threatened species continues to rise across the world (Browning et al., 2001;IPBES, 2019;IUCN, 2021;Moseby et al., 2018). Populations of mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles have declined in size by an average of 68% since the 1970s (IUCN, 2021; WWF, 2020).

Increased extinction rates and decreased abundance of remaining wild species were documented in the Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, along with severe global declines in the extent and condition of natural ecosystems (IPBES, 2019). The report attributes land and sea use changes, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution, and invasive species as key direct drivers of these declines.

The clearing of native habitat has caused decreased home ranges for some species and has placed intense pressure on populations of wild animals. Greenhouse emissions have also increased, resulting in global temperature changes, detrimental to many species. According to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN, 2021), over 5300 (10%) vertebrate species are currently endangered or critically endangered.

Conservation measures intended to limit population declines and species extinctions include habitat protection, invasive species control, translocations and breeding programs (Berger-Tal et al., 2020). Sixteen percent of the world's critically endangered vertebrates are dependent on translocation programs for survival (IUCN, 2021;Morris et al., 2021). Captive breeding programmes are crucial to many translocation programmes, providing 'fit for release' individuals as a means of establishing or supplementing wild populations (Berger-Tal et al., 2020;Morris et al., 2021).

In Australia, significant population declines, and increased extinction rates have been observed across many faunal taxa since European colonisation (Burgman et al., 2007;Ford et al., 2001;Pedler et al., 2018;Short & Smith, 1994). Australia has the highest rate of mammal extinctions of all continents (Kingsley et al., 2012;Pedler et al., 2018;Short & Smith, 1994). The effects of invasive species, combined with habitat fragmentation, changes in hydrology, land clearing for forestry, mining, farming and housing, altered fire regimes, and hunting have all contributed to Australia's high extinction rates (Bannister et al., 2016;Ceballos et al., 2015;Morrant et al., 2017;Sheean et al., 2012;White et al., 2020;Woinarski, 2016).

Globally, the risk of extinction for modern day mammal species generally increases with body size (Johnson & Isaac, 2009). This is often linked to factors such as low population density, low fecundity, and longer generation times. Larger animals are also often targeted by humans, for both food and trade, and the effects of habitat loss and fragmentation (Amir et al., 2022) can be greater for larger animals. However, in Australia, the decline and extinction of medium sized mammal species over the past 200 years has exceeded that of smaller and larger mammals (Johnson & Isaac 2009).

Australia's small to medium-sized mammals within the critical weight range (CWR) of 35-5500 g (Burbidge & McKenzie, 1989) are at a higher risk of extinction than smaller or larger mammals (Johnson & Isaac 2009;Parrott et al., 2017;Pedler et al., 2018;White et al., 2020). Species within the CWR are more susceptible to predation from introduced species (e.g. foxes and cats). Species below the CWR are generally more resilient to predation because of higher population growth rates, whereas larger species are not as vulnerable to predation by cats and foxes (Johnson & Isaac 2009). Well known examples of Australian mammal species within the CWR include: Quolls (Dasyurus sp.), bandicoots (Isoodon sp. and Perameles sp.) and bilbies (Macrotis sp.) (Fitzsimons et al., 2010;Menkhorst & Knight, 2011). Some smaller macropods also fall within the CWR, including Brush-tailed Rock Wallaby, Petrogale penicillata.

Habitat fragmentation and predation by invasive species are key drivers of biodiversity loss, especially for native Australian mammals in the CWR (Burbidge & McKenzie, 1989;Johnson & Isaac, 2009). Habitat fragmentation is the division of large, unbroken areas of habitat, into smaller, isolated habitat fragments within a landscape (Ewers & Didham, 2006). In terrestrial ecosystems, habitat fragmentation is widespread and is usually attributed to land use changes. As areas of remaining habitat become smaller and more isolated, populations of wild animals which depend on such habitat become smaller.

Many species which were once widespread now exist only in small, fragmented habitats (Ewers & Didham, 2006). Previously interconnected populations can become separated from one another because of habitat fragmentation, resulting in several smaller, isolated, populations; each of which is less viable. Smaller populations are characterised by reduced genetic diversity which can lead to inbreeding (e.g. Madsen et al., 1996;Seymour et al., 2001;Wildt et al., 1987) and may decrease the ability of a species to adapt to environmental change and pressures (Reckless et al., 2017;White et al., 2020).

The global environment is changing at an increasing rate, and many species will need to adapt to avoid an increased chance of extinction (Burbidge et al., 2011;Hoffmann & Sgró, 2011;Reckless et al., 2017). In Australia, the introduction of exotic animals is of particular concern. Introduced predators, such as the Red Fox (Vulpes vulpes) and Feral
Cat (Felis catus), prey on native wildlife; and introduced herbivores, including the European Rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus), compete with native wildlife for food resources.

The distributions of many of Australia's endemic mammals within the CWR have been reduced to small, isolated populations with reduced genetic diversity. Such populations are also experiencing changes in climatic conditions, such as: higher or lower rainfall, increased temperatures, increases in the frequency, intensity and extent of bushfires and increases in the probability of erratic weather patterns. These pressures can increase the risk of starvation, drought stress, and hyperthermia for individual animals, resulting in reduced size and viability of populations (Reckless et al., 2017;White et al., 2020).

div.head: Translocations
div.p: Interventions, including captive breeding programs and translocations are required to ensure the security of Australia's remaining mammal diversity (White et al., 2020).

Interventions intended to maintain a representative range of habitats and species are generally described as conservation interventions. In some cases, conservation interventions may not be sufficient to ensure the stability of functioning ecosystems, or to address population declines (Sheean et al., 2012). This can occur where the movement of individuals between fragmented populations is restricted, preventing the supplementation of a declining population's gene pool by migration from other nearby populations. Movement across a landscape (migration) may be prevented or limited by the absence of source populations, or by interactions between the species' biology and/or habitat requirements and the effects of habitat fragmentation (Sheean et al., 2012).
Most conservation programs are conducted in situ and aim to maintain species within their natural habitat through preservation, management and reserves (NRMMC, 2009).
Ex situ conservation programs, such as captive breeding, may be useful where wild populations are very small or extinct (Hogg, 2013;Seddon et al., 2007;Soorae, 2018).

Where natural populations are small and at serious risk of extinction, captive breeding programs can be used as a conservation tool to ensure the survival of species. Captive breeding programs can provide a source of individuals or populations to establish, reestablish or supplement wild or other captive bred populations via translocations (Hedrick & Fredrickson 2008). Additionally, captive breeding programs can establish insurance populations (which can persist in captivity when stochastic events cause the loss of wild populations) (Hedrick & Fredrickson, 2008;WWF 2007).

The term 'translocations' is used to describe movements or removal, facilitated by humans, of organisms between one area and released in either in the wild or in captivity or confinement at another area (DEECA, 2023). Translocations may be accidental (e.g. escapees) or intentional (IUCN, 2013). Intentional translocations are used to meet conservation objectives, for example, to address decreasing population sizes and the concomitant decrease in genetic potential that accompanies them (IUCN, 2013;Weeks et al., 2011); and to address concerns including: animal welfare, political, commercial, or recreational interests.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) summarises conservation translocation as: "the intentional movement and release of a living organism where the primary objective is a conservation benefit: this will usually comprise improving the conservation status of the focal species locally or globally, and/or restoring natural ecosystem functions or processes" (IUCN 2013, p. 2).

Relocation of individuals, either between captive populations, from captive populations to wild populations, or between wild populations, is a useful tool for threatened species management (Armstrong & McLean, 1995;Baker et al., 2012;Fischer & Lindenmayer, 2000;Griffith et al., 1989;Pedler et al., 2018).

The IUCN recognises several types of translocations, each with various subtypes. Table 1.1 summarises these, and contains information drawn from (IUCN 2021). "The intentional movement and release of an organism outside its indigenous range to avoid extinction of populations of the focal species"

Ecological replacement "The intentional movement and release of an organism outside its indigenous range to perform a specific ecological function" Removal = "Intentional movement of an organism from places where they are threatening human health and safety, amenity, built assets or natural or other values" Salvage = "The movement of an organism from areas subject to habitat disturbance or loss or movement of threatened fauna into captivity in an effort to prevent a further decline in conservation status" Emergency salvage "The unplanned or ad hoc translocation to a temporary or permanent holding location, triggered in response to events such as":

• an environmental crisis • occurrence of a disease/pathogen /predator, where that may result in a population being lost, or the threatened taxon becoming more vulnerable • other event deemed to be an emergency. Experimental translocations = "The translocation of selected threatened fauna for research"

Various authors have considered the successes (Baker et al., 2012;Beheregaray et al., 2021;Lyon et al., 2012;Osterberg et al., 2015;Ottewell et al., 2014;White et al., 2020) and failures (Fischer & Lindenmayer, 2000;Short et al., 1992;Watkins et al., 2018) of translocations in Australia and around the world. Some of the most highly publicised translocations include that of the Gray Wolf (Canis lupus) in Yellowstone National Park, United States of America (Smith et al., 2003), Española Giant Galapagos Tortoise (Chelonoidis hoodensis) on the Galapagos Islands in Ecuador (Gibbs et al., 2014) and European Bison (Bison bonasus) in the Southern Carpathians, Romania and Rhodope Mountains, Bulgaria (Vlasakker, 2014). Between 1914 and1926, over 130 Gray Wolves were killed in Yellowstone National Park and in 1926 the last reported pack of Gray Wolves was observed although singular wolf sightings persisted (National Parks Service, 2022). As the primary prey of the Gray Wolf is Elk (Cervus canadensis) and other ungulate species, the removal of wolves from Yellowstone National Park caused a trophic cascade leading to an increased fecundity in ungulate species and thus increased herbivory, and a decrease in resources for scavenging carnivores. In 1995 and 1996, 41 wild Gray Wolves from Canada and northwestern Montana were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park (National Parks Service, 2022). Since their translocation, the healthy populations of this top-order keystone predator have been sustained within the park, with a positive impact on vegetation recovery (National Parks Service, 2022;Smith et al., 2003).

Like the Gray Wolf, the European Bison is considered a keystone species. (Rewilding Europe, 2021). The species was declared extinct in the wild in 1927. At the time, there were less than 60 individuals in captivity (Vlasakker, 2014). The first reintroduction of European Bison into the wild occurred in 1952 (Vlasakker, 2014) in the Southern Carpathians region, Bulgaria. More than 200 breeding centres now exist in Europe, supporting over 1200 individuals (around 30% of the total global population) (Vlasakker, 2014). The Bison's diet contains mostly grasses, but they also consume several bush, shrub, and tree species (Vlasakker, 2014). Each individual can consume up to 60 kg of food each day and the species plays a significant role in creating a mosaic of vegetation types in the landscape via their foraging activities (Vlasakker, 2014). As large herbivores, they also heavily influence nitrogen turnover within an ecosystem by eating plants and redistributing nitrogen via urination and defecation (Vlasakker, 2014).

One of the most successful examples of conservation via species translocation is that of the Española Giant Galapagos Tortoise. Once numbering in the thousands, the population of Española Giant Galapagos Tortoise was reduced to just 14 wild individuals by the 1960s (Gibbs et al., 2014). These 14 wild individuals (2 males and 12 females), and a captive male, "Diego", were the founders of a captive breeding program that continued for 50 years (Galapagos Conservancy, 2022;Gibbs et al., 2014). There is currently a stable population of around 2300 Española Giant Galapagos Tortoises in the wild (Galapagos Conservancy 2022; Gibbs et al., 2014). Because of the success of the captive breeding and reintroduction program, which occurred with concurrent habitat conservation, this captive breeding program ceased in 2020 (Galapagos Conservancy 2022; Gibbs et al., 2014).
All of these species were extinct in the wild, or close to extinction, but have now recovered due to successful translocation programs (Gibbs et al., 2014;Smith et al., 2003;Vlasakker, 2014).

Translocation has been used as an active conservation tool in Australia since the 1880s (Armstrong & McLean, 1995;Short, 2009). An analysis by Short (2009) found more than 380 instances of faunal translocation within Australia. These 380 examples, represented 100 species of mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians (Short, 2009). Sixty-five per cent of these translocations were "reintroductions", 22% were "conservation introductions" and 13% were "reinforcements" (Short, 2009). Most of these translocations have involved marsupials, but in recent years, a wider variety of vertebrate, invertebrate and plant species have been translocated (Short, 2009).

Translocations are conducted across a wide range of ecosystems, climates, and locations, by various organisations and individuals, including government, conservation organisations, ecologists, wildlife carers and the public. Some of the earliest records of translocations in Australia include movements of Koalas (Short, 2009). In all cases, these translocations occurred in response to concerns about dwindling mainland populations of these species.

More recently, translocations have played fundamental roles in the successful establishment of populations of many other species in Australia, including the Burrowing Bettong (Bettongia lesueur) (Short & Turner, 2000), Brush-tailed Bettong or Woylie (Bettongia penicillata) (Short, 2009) and the Tammar Wallaby (Short, 2009). Griffith et al. (1989) states that a translocation is successful if it results in a selfsustaining population in the wild. Although this is one measure of success, the New South Wales Translocation Operational Policy (2019) advises that each translocation program should have a set of criteria against which success is measured and monitored.

The Australian Capital Territory (ACT) Government's Conservator Guidelines for the Translocation of Native Flora and Fauna (2017) also recommend the identification of an exit strategy with an evaluation framework that defines either the failure or success of each program. Persistence of success over longer time scales also needs to be considered (Fischer & Lindenmayer, 2000;Short, 2009).

div.head: Associated with the Australian Government's Environment Protection and Biodiversity
div.p: Conservation (EPBC) Act (1999), the EPBC Act Policy Statement on the Translocation of Listed Threatened Species (Australian Government, 2013, p. 7) states that, when evaluating the long-term success of any species translocation, each program needs to "address the genetic, demographic, and size parameters of populations; the security and relative contribution to the conservation of the entity as a whole, and the nature and sustainability of the population's long-term interaction with the receiving environment". Short (2009) estimated that in Australia, 32% of translocation programs were successful, 28% unsuccessful, and for 40%, outcomes were unknown. Predation (mostly from foxes (Vulpes vulpes), cats (Felis catus), dingoes (Canis familiaris dingo) and avian predators) was identified as the primary reason for failure in 45 (43%) of the 105 cases that had demonstrably failed (Short, 2009). A review by Fischer & Lindenmayer (2000), of translocations across the world, found that translocation programs in Australia and New Zealand had higher failure rates compared to those in the United States of America. A more recent review by Morris et al. (2021) found that translocations in Oceania were more likely to fail, compared to those in Europe and North America. Morris et al. (2021) attributed the higher failure rates in Australia and New Zealand to the higher prevalence of invasive species in this region.
Measuring the success of translocation programs is not always linear, and multiple factors need to be taken into consideration when establishing indicators for success.

Various authors have attempted to identify attributes of translocation programs within Australia, across several different species, that can influence success. Appendix 1 provides a summary of these. In the Australian context, selection of appropriate reintroduction sites, a good understanding of habitat requirements and consideration of the risk of predation is important (Appendix 1).

Translocations of animals into poor or unsuitable habitat are more likely to fail (Griffith et al., 1989;Moorhouse et al., 2009;Moseby et al., 2020). Sites at which individuals are to be released are usually assessed for habitat quality prior to the translocation event (Griffith et al., 1989;Moorhouse et al., 2009;Moseby et al., 2020). Variations in habitat quality at prospective release sites can be a result of vegetation clearance, pest species introduction, fragmentation, and inappropriate fire regimes. It has been suggested that poor quality habitat is associated with increased predation rates, or less availability or poorer quality shelter, refuge and forage; all of which can contribute to failed translocations (Bennett et al., 2013;Doherty et al., 2015;Moseby et al., 2020;Woinarski et al., 2015). Areas that are more physically disturbed and open are known to attract predators (Gill et al., 2014;Luck et al., 1999;Towerton et al., 2011).

Habitat quality at a particular location can be assessed by considering the presence of physical attributes such as food and refugia, as well as the possibility of restricted use of these resources due to predation and competition (Johnson, 2005;Moseby et al., 2020).

Where the species of interest is present and accessible, habitat quality can also be inferred by comparing individual or population parameters across locations (Moseby et al., 2020). Such parameters may include body condition, survival, growth rates, and reproduction.

div.head: Habitat Suitability Models (HSM) to identify suitable release locations for translocated animals
div.p: Translocation programs are used in species conservation, but their success rates, particularly in Australia, are low (Fischer & Lindenmayer, 2000;Short, 2009). Lack of information about habitat requirements, especially for rare and endangered species, is commonly cited to explain poor outcomes for translocation programs (appendix 1). In order to address this, the identification of suitable release sites using analytical methods such as habitat suitability models, has become common (e.g. Carroll et al., 2003;Cook et al., 2010;Merrill et al., 1999;Wilson et al., 2011).

Habitat Suitability Models (hereafter 'HSM') also known as species distribution models, compare observations, such as presence (e.g. MaxEnt models), or presence/absence, data to a set of environmental variables that can represent key factors defining a species' ecological niche (Elith & Leathwick, 2009;Guisan & Zimmermann, 2000;Hirzel et al., 2006).

Habitat Suitability Models (HSM) have been used, world-wide, to identify potential translocation sites for a variety of species. These include Freshwater Pearl Mussels (Margaritifera margaritifera) in Northern Ireland (Wilson et al., 2011), European Bison (Bison bonasus) (Bleyhl et al., 2015;Lord et al., 2020), American Beaver (Castor canadensi) (Baldwin, 2013), White-rumped Vulture (Gyps bengalensis) in India (Anoop et al., 2020) and Eastern Barred Bandicoot (Perameles gunnii) in Australia (Cook et al., 2010). The use of HSM in plant translocations has also been proven to result in higher germination success post-translocation (Draper et al., 2019).

Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are the preferred tool with which to construct HSM (Guisan & Zimmermann, 2000;Wilson et al., 2011). GIS can be used to create spatial datasets displaying the configuration of suitable habitat (Gibson et al., 2004;Guisan & Zimmermann, 2000). GIS models are generally based on remote-sensed satellite data and tend to only represent larger scale factors for HSM (Guisan & Zimmermann, 2000;Wilson et al., 2011).
The quality of HSM is dependent on the quality of the input variables. Making informed decisions in selecting the types of variables used in models is challenging, but essential.

div.head: Structured Decision Making (SDM)
div.p: Since biodiversity losses are predicted to increase in the future (Browning et al., 2001;IPBES 2019;IUCN 2021Moseby et al., 2018), effective strategies to reduce species decline are required (Anderson et al., 2021). Evidence-based decisions and scientific data to support conservation decision-making is paramount (Taylor et al., 2017).

Structured Decision Making (hereafter 'SDM') is a methodological technique used to make informed decisions in complex environments. Structured Decision Making (SDM) allows decision makers to organise complex issues in "ways that helps individuals and groups build common understanding, identify relevant information and find innovative solutions to difficult environmental problems" (Gregory et al. 2012, p. ix). Structured Decision Making (SDM) can be applied using a group of experts to find solutions in a rigorous, inclusive, defensible and transparent way (Gregory et al., 2012).

The foundations of SDM are based on the premise that good decisions are made when there is an in-depth understanding of what is important (values) and what is likely to happen if a particular decision, or its alternative, is implemented (consequences) (Gregory et al., 2012). Structured Decision Making involves a six-step process (Figure 1.1) that can be applied to any environmental management decision (Gregory et al., 2012). Figure 1.1 has been adapted from Gregory et al. (2012) and is relevant to selecting key habitat attributes for use in HSM for Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies (BTRW) (Chapter 2). Structured Decision Making (SDM) is a valuable tool for land managers and in ecological science where "competing objectives, uncertainty surrounding the available management options, and/or high uncertainty about the consequences of management is needed" (DELWP 2019, p. 1). This process can identify uncertainty that exists in data, and assist in recognising uncertainties in making management decisions (Gregory et al., 2012;DELWP, 2019).

div.head: Structured Decision Making (SDM) used to inform translocations
div.p: Structured Decision Making (SDM) has been increasingly used to inform decisions surrounding natural resource management (Gregory et al., 2012), but is an underutilised method used in translocation decisions (Panfylova et al., 2019;Taylor et al., 2017). Any A small population remained two years after the initial translocation in 2013, but the mortality rates for females was high (Panfylova et al., 2019). Questions surrounding whether more females should be released was raised (Panfylova et al., 2019). Panfylova et al. (2019) study used SDM to evaluate the feasibility of translocating an addition 15 females to the remaining population. The discussions around this particular translocation was complex, but decision makers were able to make an informed decision using SDM, of no further translocations (Panfylova et al., 2019).

Structured Decision Making (SDM) has also been used by land managers to inform decisions around whether or not releasing captive-reared Whooping Crane (Grus Americana) chicks would help in the recovery of the non-migratory population in Florida (Converse et al., 2013). Converse et al. (2013) suggested that best choice among many of the alternatives identified for achieving the management objectives was to release three groups of captive-reared chicks per year for 10 years.
Other examples of the application of SDM to inform translocation decisions include the development of the Flatwood Salamanders (Ambystoma cingulatum and A. cingulatum)

recovery plans (O'Donnell et al., 2017); and identifying the best translocation strategy for the Bull Trout (Salvelinus confluentus) in northwest America, with the goal of maximizing the number of adults at the translocation population without reducing the source population (Brignon et al., 2018).

div.head: Macropod translocations
div.p: Within Australia, translocations of macropod species have had limited success (Short et al., 1992). Challenges have included a lack of knowledge of target species biology and their habitat requirements; inadequate planning, inappropriate or inaccurate site selection, lack of predator control and a lack of continuous monitoring (Finlayson et al., 2008;Molyneux, 2010;Short, 2009;Short et al., 1992). Factors such as the presence of refuges, resource availability, connectivity, climate, presence of predators, competition, and other species interactions can all influence translocation success (Molyneux, 2010;Taggart et al., 2008). A multi-faceted approach is essential in identifying the relationships between each species and their environment (Fischer & Lindenmayer, 2000;Short, 2009;Taggart et al., 2015).

div.head: Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (BTRW) (Petrogale penicillata)
div.p: Some macropod species are widespread and occur across many different habitat types and climates. When attempting to understand habitat use, each species must be examined across its entire range and at a site level scale. The rock-wallabies, genus Petrogale, are an example of a highly specialised macropod group (Molyneux, 2010).

There are approximately 30 species of wallaby, including 16 species of rock-wallaby in Australia (Menkhorst & Knight, 2011). The Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (BTRW), Petrogale penicillata, is one of the largest, though still within the CWR for predation by introduced cats and foxes. Adult BTRW range between 5-11 kg (males) and 4-8 kg (females) (Menkhorst & Knight, 2011). Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies (BTRW) are extremely agile and can move through steep, rocky, rugged areas with precision (Hill & Baker-Gabb, 2003), showing a preference for highly complex rocky environments (Malam, 2012;Short, 1982;Taggart et al., 2008;).

div.head: Cultural significance
div.p: Wallabies are considered both culturally and spiritually significant in Indigenous Australian culture. They feature in Dreaming Stories across Australia (AGDAWE, 2021;Bush Heritage, 2022). The name Wallaby is derived from the Eora word, "Wulaba" of the Eora people from coastal New South Wales (AGDAWE 2021).

div.head: Previous distribution
div.p: Once widely distributed across the mountainous country of south-eastern Australia (Figure 1.2), the distribution of BTRW has contracted, particularly within the southern extent of their range (Figure 1.3) (Short & Milkovits, 1990). Previously, BTRW existed (Grampians National Park, or 'the Grampians') suggest that these locations have been past strongholds for BTRW (Wakefield, 1954(Wakefield, , 1971)). Genetic similarities between the extant populations in East Gippsland and Gariwerd, as well as fossil records and anecdotal evidence, suggest that there was historically a continuous distribution throughout Victoria (Browning et al., 2001;Lunney et al., 1996;Malam, 2012;Paplinska et al., 2011).

div.head: Present distribution
div.p: The decline of the NESU populations has been less severe than that of the CESU and SESU populations (Delaney et al., 2005). It is estimated that the geographic range of the BTRW has been reduced by 50-90% since European colonisation (Short & Milkovits, 1990). It is believed that around 80% of the global population of the BTRW is within north-eastern New South Wales and south-eastern Queensland (Woinarski & Burbidge, 2016). It is considered that the quality of habitat in the north is generally higher, the northern populations are larger with good gene flow, and predation appears to be lower (Delaney et al., 2005).

The last wild sighting of the BTRW in the ACT was in 1959 (ACT Governement, 2021). In 1999 the last remaining BTRW was removed from Gariwerd (the Grampians) and transferred into captivity (Taggart et al., 2015). There are now only two wild populations in Victoria: East Gippsland (on Gunaikurnai Country) and a reintroduced population comprising individuals of both SESU and CESU heritage in Gariwerd. There are no extant wild populations in the ACT (ACT Government, 2021;Ormay, 1996). As of June 2022
there were approximately 45 individuals in the East Gippsland population (Gaborov, 2022) and between 8-10 individuals in Gariwerd (Kleemann, 2019;M.Perri personal communication, 2021).

div.head: Extralimital distribution
div.p: Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (BTRW) populations exist outside of Australia as a result of both accidental (Hawaii, U.S.A) (Eldridge & Browning, 2002;Lazell et al., 1984) and intentional (New Zealand) releases (Eldridge et al., 2001). It is considered a pest species in both New Zealand and Hawaii.

div.head: Threats/Reasons for Decline
div.p: Like many other species within the CWR, BTRW is susceptible to introduced threats such as predation from introduced species (Table 1.3). Other threats from historical persecution/hunting, habitat decline, competition from introduced mammal species, genetic decline and climate change are responsible for the decline in BTRW populations across Australia (Table 1.3).

Events due to climate change such as increase prevalence of drought and altered fire regimes, pose a serious threat to all species, particularly small, fragmented populations, such as BTRW (Delaney et al., 2005;Lunney et al., 1996;Malam, 2012;Taggart et al., 2008). During times of drought and vegetation loss due to bushfires, BTRW often forage over greater distances in order to access food and water resources (Malam, 2012). This in turn may expose rock-wallabies to greater predation risk because individuals venture further from their refuge Dovey et al., (2002); Gaborov & Corrigan, (2019) Lobert & Waters, (1988a); Lunney et al., (1996); Malam, (2012); Menkhorst & Hynes, (2010); Molyneux et al., (2011);Taggart et al., (2008).

div.p: Despite small and highly fragmented populations, particularly in the southern part of its range, the BTRW is widely distributed across Eastern Australia. Its distribution across

div.head: Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby translocations in Victoria
div.p: The Southern Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (SBTRW) is the only rock-wallaby found in Victoria and the rarest of all the Evolutionary Significant Units (ESU) (Gaborov 2021;Hazlitt et al., 2014) (Figure 1.2). The genetic diversity of this ESU has declined significantly. This has led to selective hybridisation of the SBTRW with the central BTRW (CBTRW) in captive breeding programs (Gaborov, 2021(Gaborov, , 2022)). Founder wallabies were bred in captivity, crossing the SESU gene pool (75%) with the CESU (25%) (Gaborov, 2021(Gaborov, , 2022)). These hybrid animals are now being used in the SBTRW captive breeding program at Mount Rothwell Conservation and Research Reserve and Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve (TNR).

Between 2008 -2012, 39 hybrid (SESU and CESU) BTRW were translocated into Gariwerd (Grampians National Park) Moora Moora site (Taggart et al., 2015). As of 2015, only 18% survived (Taggart et al., 2015). Of the animals of which did not survive, 15% died due to predation (Taggart et al., 2015). Since 2012, no individuals have been translocated into Gariwerd.

As of autumn 2023, 11 BTRW have been translocated into Little River Gorge, Victoria (Gaborov, 2023). Two males were released in September 2019; one female and three males were released in September 2020; two males and three females were released in October 2022 (Gaborov, 2021(Gaborov, , 2022 ) ). When surveyed in autumn 2023, a total of five (four females and one male) of the 11 translocated individuals were recorded on camera (Gaborov, 2023). All three females translocated in 2022 were recorded and one male and one female translocated in 2019 were recorded in Little River Gorge, Victoria.

div.head: Anticipated contribution of the current study to existing knowledge
div.p: While previous studies have assessed and surveyed BTRW habitat around Australia (Table 1.5), only Taggart et al. (2008) and Clausen (2011) have assessed and nominated sites for BTRW translocations in Victoria. Those studies used a point-score system and nominated sites which resulted in limited translocation success. This project aims to expand on previous studies and fill significant gaps in the knowledge of site selection for BTRW translocations in both Victoria and the ACT.
This study differs from previous studies in its use of an explicit decision-making process adapted from Gregory et al., (2012) at two key stages:
1. to inform the selection of habitat attributes for a HSM, and 2. to inform the recommendation of suitable release sites following modelling.

The explicit decision-making process method involves collaboration with field experts, academics, and generalists to address a series of problems and questions which can be applied to various investigations and scenarios. It is intended that the use of an explicit decision-making process in this study will provide researchers and land managers with more confidence in the final recommendation of potential release locations and lead to greater success for the SBTRW recovery program.
Purpose and significance of the research -aims; objectives; research questions?

This project contributes to a major reintroduction program of an iconic threatened species: Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (Petrogale penicillata) (BRTW). A range of stakeholders are involved with, and have contributed funding for, this project. These include Zoos Victoria, the Victorian Government Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DECCA), the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) Government's

Environment, Planning and Sustainable Development Directorate and the Southern Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (SBTRW) Recovery Team. The Recovery Team is responsible for implementing the National Recovery Plan (Menkhorst & Hynes, 2010) for the species in Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory (ACT).

The objectives of the Recovery Team, over the next five years, are to increase the number of animals in extant and captive bred populations, and to translocate captivebred individuals to suitable locations to establish new BTRW colonies in Victoria and the ACT.

This project will build on previous studies to identify sites in eastern Victoria and the ACT which have a high probability of supporting successful establishment of new BTRW colonies. In doing so, the project contributes to the objectives of the National Recovery Plan (Menkhorst & Hynes, 2010).
Specifically, this project will:
1. Review the literature to identify key habitat requirements for BTRW and describe these as habitat variables (Chapter 1).

2. Use a panel of experts and an explicit decision-making process adapted from Gregory et al., (2012) to evaluate the importance of each habitat variable in determining habitat suitability for new BTRW colonies (Chapter 2).

3. Use Geographic Information System (GIS) methods, remote sensing data and MaxEnt software, to develop a Habitat Suitability Model for BTRW at multiple spatial scales, based on the key variables identified by the explicit decisionmaking process (Chapter 3).
4. Use the Habitat Suitability Model to identify a shortlist of candidate sites (Chapter 3).
5. Use a panel of experts and an explicit decision-making process to rank those candidate sites for ground-truthing (Chapter 4).
6. Ground-truth and use fine scale habitat preferences to create a final list of candidate sites for the establishment of new BTRW colonies in Victoria and the ACT (Chapter 4).

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Native Australian mammal species within the CWR (35-5500 g) (Burbidge & McKenzie, 1989) are at a higher risk of extinction than other Australian mammal groups (Johnson & Isaac, 2009;Parrott et al., 2017;Pedler et al. 2018;White et al. 2020). Interventions, such as captive breeding programs, translocations, habitat preservation, research, community education and introduced species management are needed to ensure the security of Australia's remaining mammal diversity (White et al., 2020). The distributions of many of Australia's endemic mammals within the CWR, including BTRW, have been reduced to small, isolated populations with reduced genetic diversity (Reckless et al., 2017;White et al., 2020).

For BTRW populations around Australia, translocations of captive bred individuals to newly established wild populations are a key future conservation strategy. The identification of suitable translocation release sites is an important step in implementing this strategy.

Understanding key habitat preferences is paramount in the success of any translocation program. The use of an explicit decision-making process (Gregory et al., 2012) is an appropriate approach to identify key habitat variables for inclusion in a Habitat Suitability Model for SBTRW in Victoria and ACT and to inform the recommendation of suitable release sites predicted by such a model. The use of an explicit decision-making process to aid in the process of identifying model variables, will provide researchers and land managers with more confidence in the final recommendation of potential release locations and is likely to lead to greater success for the SBTRW recovery program.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Unlike other macropod species that occupy a broad range of niches, Rock-wallabies are limited to habitats that are highly complex and occur sporadically throughout the landscape (Ruykys, 2011). Petrogale sp. occurrence is patchy even within their geographical niche suggesting that fine-scale habitat selection is a factor and restriction to current suitable habitat is unlikely to be due to post-colonisation factors (Ruykys, 2011). For Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (BTRW) populations around Australia, translocations of captive bred individuals to newly established wild populations are a key future and contemporary conservation strategy. The identification of suitable translocation release sites is an important step in implementing this strategy.
Understanding key habitat preferences is paramount in BTRW persistence; and the ease with which threats such as predation can be managed.

div.head: Structured Decision Making (SDM) -an adapted approach
div.p: Species conservation decisions can be difficult, especially within an environmental management context. Structured Decision Making is typically used to select among alternative management strategies (Gregory et al., 2012;DELWP, 2019).

However, the SDM method can be applied to other complex decisions involving selecting among discrete alternatives using a group of expert participants. Habitat variable selection for translocations, via a recovery team, is often done informally, and SDM offers a good alternative in a group decision environment.

The use of an adapted Structured Decision Making (SDM) process (Gregory et al., 2012) to inform the creation of a Habitat Suitability Model (HSM) is an appropriate approach to identify key habitat variables for inclusion in a HSM for Southern Brush-tailed Rockwallabies (SBTRW) in Victoria and Australian Capital Territory (ACT) and to inform the recommendation of suitable release sites predicted by such a model.

The use of an adapted SDM approach to aid in the process of identifying model variables (habitat attributes), will provide researchers and land managers with more confidence in the final recommendation of potential release locations and lead to greater success for the SBTRW recovery program. The foundations of SDM are based on the premise that good decisions are made when there is an in-depth understanding of what is important (values) and what is likely to happen if a particular decision, or its alternative, is implemented (consequences) (Gregory et al., 2012).

The SDM process usually involves a facilitated Workshop, engaging with, for example, stakeholders, scientists, community members and government. As described in Chapter 1, SDM involves a six step process (Figure 1.1 and Table 2.1) that can be applied to any environmental management decision (Gregory et al., 2012). Defining objectives and performance criteria, identifying and assessing alternatives, and having a clear understanding of uncertainties and trade-offs are all key elements in the SDM process (Gregory et al., 2012;Hemming et al., 2021) (Table 2.1).

div.head: Objectives and performance measures
div.p: Defining "what matters" (objectives) and the metrics used for assessing how alternatives perform regarding the objectives (performance measures).

div.head: Alternatives
div.p: After the problem, objectives, and performance measures have been identified, the next step is to identify alternatives. Consequences An estimation of the alternative consequences against the performance measures.

div.head: Trade-offs
div.p: Define and weigh alternatives that achieve a balance across all objectives. Decisions Includes a review and, revisitation if needed of any aspect of the SDM process.

To date, research into the habitat requirements of BTRW has mainly been focussed on NESU populations in New South Wales (NSW) and Queensland (QLD), with little to no focus on the SESU in Victoria and the ACT (Table 1.5). Important exceptions are in Gariwerd (the Grampians) where early studies were focused (Malam, 2012;Lobert & Waters, 1988a, 1988b;Taggart et al., 2008) (Table 1.5). Chapter 3 provides more information on the application of HSM's and the predicted distribution of BTRW.

Most modelling of potential BTRW habitat has been done solely on the basis of habitat attributes and has not involved expert elicitation (Ashcroft et al., 2014;Malam, 2012;Morris et al., 2020;Murray et al., 2011;Thurtell et al., 2021). This project will differ from previous studies by using experts from the SBTRW Recovery Team and other BTRW Recovery Team experts from NSW and QLD, to make an informed decision on habitat attributes required for BTRW survival using an explicit decision-making process based on SDM .

The SBTRW Recovery Team consists of representatives from the Australian Capital Territory Government -threatened species team, Zoos Victoria, the Victorian Government's Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA), Parks Victoria (PV), Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve (TNR), Mount Rothwell Conservation and Research Reserve, and several university experts with significant expertise in SBTRW ecology, and recovery. The Recovery Team is responsible for implementing the National Recovery Plan (Menkhorst & Hynes, 2010) and the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Action Statement (Hill & Baker-Gabb, 2003) for the Southern ESU in Victoria and the ACT. The objectives of the Recovery Team, over the next five years, are to increase the number of animals in extant and captive bred populations, and to translocate captive-bred individuals to suitable locations to establish new BTRW colonies in Victoria and the ACT.

In this Chapter expert elicitation and an explicit decision-making process will be used to identify key habitat and management attributes associated with BTRW occupancy. These attributes will be ranked and later used to inform a Habitat Suitability Model (HSM) (Chapter 3).

div.head: Methods: explicit decision-making Workshop 1identifying habitat attributes
div.p: The work presented in this Chapter, and in Chapters 3 and 4, was undertaken with the approval of the Federation University Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC approval: B21-142).

Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (BTRW) experts were informally invited to participate in two explicit decision-making Workshops during a meeting of the SBTRW Recovery Team on the 23 rd of November 2021, at which a presentation outlining this project was made.

Other BTRW experts from around Australia, who did not attend the SBTRW Recovery Team meeting, were notified about the project, and invited to contact the researcher, by attendees of the meeting. Later, a formal invitation to participate in the project was sent to attendees of the meeting and other BTRW experts from NSW and QLD who had expressed interest in participating. The formal invitation included an explanatory statement and a consent form which can be viewed online (HERE).

The BTRW experts were invited to contribute to the work described in this Chapter, and the work described in Chapter 4. That is, they were invited to participate in two explicit decision-making Workshops. First, a habitat attribution identification Workshop was held to establish a consensus among the group about the most important habitat attributes for BTRW. Outcomes of this first Workshop are reported in this Chapter. Once identified, these habitat attributes were used in modelling potential release sites, reported in Chapter 3. During a second Workshop, which was followed by some independent decision making by the experts, participants provided expert feedback on the model output. The outcomes of the explicit decision-making Workshop 2, and the subsequent independent decision making of participants, are reported in Chapter 4.

Workshops were held via videoconferencing due to the high incidence of Covid 19 in the community at the time of the meetings. This proved to be advantageous because several representatives from Victoria, ACT, NSW and QLD were able to participate in these Workshops without a requirement for travel.

Prior to Workshop 1 -identifying habitat attributes, a list of example objectives and performance criteria was identified (Table 2.2) using the SDM methodology described by Gregory et al. (2012) with the assistance of DEECA Natural Environmental Program Regional Manager, Dr Lucas Bluff and the supervisory group. These were examined in the explicit decision-making Workshop 1 for habitat attributes and a list of habitat and management attributes were measured against these.

The explicit decision-making Workshop 1 -identifying habitat attributes, was held on the 14 th of December 2021 via Microsoft Teams. This was a half day, online, meeting, attended by 15 BTRW experts from around Australia and was facilitated by EM. This was an open discussion where experts were asked to express their opinions on both the objectives and performance criteria previously identified and to discuss and identify the key habitat attributes contributing to BTRW survival. Experts were also asked to discuss alternatives, consequences and trade-offs associated with the habitat attributes identified, but there was confusion among participants, therefore the Structured Decision Making (SDM) approach was adapted.

A discussion around habitat attributes was had among the participants and it was decided that habitat attributes should be classified as either physical attributes or management attributes. Physical attributes were used to develop the HSM and management attributes were used in the ground-truthing process. Once the final performance criteria were identified there was a lengthy discussion around which habitat attributes are required for BTRW survival. A table outlining agreed objectives, performance criteria and key habitat attributes was developed during this process (Table 2.3).

Following the meeting, participants were contacted via email with a request to independently review and rank each of the habitat attributes (both physical and management attributes) listed in Table 2.3 from most to least important, against each of the five performance criteria listed in Table 2.3. Participants were asked to give each attribute a ranking between 0 -10.

All results were collated and the sum, mean, median, standard deviation, variance, maximum and minimum of the rankings for each physical attribute were calculated across all performance criteria using Minitab software (Minitab, 2022). Each attribute was given a ranking based on its overall mean (Tables 2.4, 2.6, 2.8 & 2.9).

The highest ranked physical attributes (Table 2.8) identified in this Chapter were used to develop the Habitat Suitability Model (HSM) described in Chapter 3. The highest ranked management attributes (Table 2.9) identified in this Chapter were used to filter sites identified via the HSM (described in Chapter 4).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: An explicit decision-making process based on Structured Decision Making (SDM) was used to identify and rank key physical and management attributes associated with BTRW.
Incorporating the opinions of 10 BTRW experts from a number of different states and agencies has given this study a greater insight into the habitat attributes BTRW require to survive in the wild.
A total of six physical and nine management attributes were identified as associated with BTRW distribution and ranked from most to least important (Tables 2.8 & 2.9).

These attributes inform the work described in Chapters 3 and 4 which use further expert elicitation and ground-truthing in conjunction with model outputs to identify the most suitable release sites for captive bred BTRW.

div.head: Physical attributes
div.p: The six physical attributes identified in Workshop 1 were ranked from most to least important as follows: Rock complexity; Distance to water; Slope; Vegetation; Elevation;
Aspect. These physical attributes were used to inform the Habitat Suitability Model (HSM) described in Chapter 3.

Experts considered rock complexity to have the greatest influence over BTRW distribution within both Victoria and the ACT (Table 2.8). This result supports previous observations suggesting that rock complexity has the greatest influence, above any other attribute, on BTRW distribution across Australia (Lobert & Waters, 1988a, 1988b;Malam, 2012;Morris et al., 2020;Murray et al. 2008Murray et al. , 2011Murray et al. , 2009;;Short, 1982;Waldegrave-Knight, 2002). Ledges, overhangs, and outcrops found in areas with high rock complexity creates connectivity within a landscape which allows individuals to move between otherwise geographically isolated colonies (Murray et al., 2008). Rock complexity also provide refuge and microclimates that can act as buffers against predation and stochastic environmental events (Waldegrave-Knight, 2002). Refuges can provide shaded areas, reducing heat stress and water loss while caves and crevices afford protection from extreme cold or wet conditions (Waldegrave-Knight, 2002).

Experts ranked distance to water as the second most important physical attribute (Table 2.8). Although, as described in Chapter 4, experts differed in their opinions about whether water has a huge influence over BTRW occupancy. The importance of distance to water has to BTRW is also poorly understood in the literature (Lobert & Waters, 1988a;Malam, 2012). Rocky habitat can provide crevices, pools and soaks which can store and provide water sources for rock-wallabies (Malam, 2012;Tuft et al., 2011). This may reduce predation risk, because it eliminates the need for rock-wallabies to venture away from rocky refuge, to areas that are less complex with free running water (Carter & Goldizen, 2003;Malam, 2012;Taggart et al., 2008;Tuft et al., 2011). Taggart et al. (2008) suggests that BTRW exhibit strong preferences for areas with permanent water sources such as rivers or creeks. These areas and their associated riparian vegetation provide forage as well as reliable sources of drinking water that facilitates breeding and shelter, supporting successful breeding at a single colony scale (Taggart et al., 2008).

Distance to water has also been shown to impact the dispersal patterns and movement of BTRW (Taggart et al., 2008). Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies are less likely to disperse and colonise new areas of suitable habitat if a permanent water source is not available. This decrease in movement in turn leads to reduced gene flow and increased inbreeding within isolated populations (Taggart et al., 2005).

There is also evidence suggesting that the moisture content contained within the diet of many rock-wallaby species may be sufficient enough (Malam, 2012). Studies into two semi-arid species (P. lateralis and P. xanthopus celeris) observed that individuals persisted for several months without requiring free water (Lapidge & Munn, 2011;Malam, 2012;Nagy & Bradshaw, 2000).

Ranked as the third most important physical attribute in this study, the importance of slope for BTRW occurrence varies in the literature. A study by Short (1982) found slope to have little influence on BTRW site occupancy, whereas Murray et al., (2011) found a strong influence of slope on BTRW occupancy.

Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies are known to consume a diverse range of foods (Tuft et al., 2011;Van Eeden et al., 2011). Exposed rocky habitats support a greater diversity of drought tolerant plant species than their nearby counterparts (Rafiee et al., 2022). Plant species that are adapted to and colonise disjunct habitats may provide a source of forage that is less influenced by climactic and hydrological variables due to their drought tolerance (Porembski et al., 2000). As global climates change and impact vegetation across different bands of elevation, the non-selective grazing behaviour exhibited by BTRW and the positive correlation between their distribution and areas of high rock complexity, with its related stochastically resistant foraging potential, may provide them with greater resilience to changing climates.

Previous studies have shown elevation to have some influence on BTRW site occupancy, but this attribute has not been reported as highly influential (e.g. Murray et al., 2008Murray et al., , 2011;;Thurtell, 2022;Thurtell et al., 2021). Currently, BTRW are known to occupy/have previously occupied areas below the snow line. Under future climatic change predictions, species are predicted to shift their current known home ranges, towards lower longitudes and higher altitudes (Couet et al., 2022).

The physical attribute that ranked the least important in terms of BTRW occupancy was aspect. Some experts posited that a north/north-eastern facing aspect is critical for BTRW (Appendix 2). A study by Waldegrave-Knight (2002) found existing BTRW sites in eastern Gippsland tended to face a north-easterly direction and extinct sites in a more north-westerly direction. Sites facing in a north easterly direction are likely to receive more sunlight in the winter months in south-eastern Australia. A study predicting the distribution of BTRW using MaxEnt modelling in Oxley Wild Rivers National Park, NSW found aspect to have little influence over the models performance, compared to other attributes (Thurtell et al., 2021).

div.head: Management attributes
div.p: The nine management attributes identified in this Workshop were ranked from most to least important as follows: Predation risk; Management access; Land tenure; Fire (scale and frequency); Fire management; Climate; Proximity to private land; Rock climbers and walkers; Historic presence of Quolls. The management attributes identified in this Chapter (predation, access and land tenure) were used to inform the ground-truthing methods used in Chapter 4.

Predation risk was the highest ranking management attribute. Predation from introduced predators such as the European Red Fox (Vulpes vulpes) and the Feral Cat (Felis catus) is considered one of the major factors in the decline of, and the major ongoing threat to BTRW (Table 1.3). Taggart et al. (2015) reviewed the primary causes of BTRW mortality within the Moora Moora colonyfoot_1 . They found that predation accounted for approximately 83.4% of the total mortalities (Taggart et al., 2015). Managing predators, particularly foxes and cats is vital for the maintenance of populations, and the establishment of translocated populations in the wild.

Management access ranked second of all the management attributes. Management access to BTRW colonies is essential. Sites need to be accessed in both a safe and timely manner. Access needs to be difficult enough that predator species are challenged in accessing the sites, while still allowing managers to access the site for translocations, monitoring, and predator control.

Land tenure was also a highly ranked management attribute. It is essential to identify sites on protected public land when considering the establishment of new BTRW colonies. Establishing colonies at sites on private property may lead to difficulties related to permissions for ongoing management access and to matters relating to ongoing land use and protection.

Fire (scale and frequency) and fire management are important factors influencing BTRW survival. Fires can destroy colonies directly and/or lead to post-fire starvation (Hill, 2022). Bushfires have been known be the primary cause of local BTRW extinction at Mt Seldom Seen, Victoria (Hill, 2022). After the 2019/2022 bushfires, several populations of BTRW in NSW required supplementary feeding to avoid starvation.

Experts considered that proximity to private land, the use of sites by rock climbers and walkers and the historic presence of Quolls had little to no influence over BTRW survival and were not important factors to take into account when identifying suitable BTRW translocation sites.

div.head: Learnings
div.p: While the initial intention of this study was to use Structured Decision Making (SDM) as it is strictly defined, the process became too difficult due confusion among participants, limits in spatial data availability, and complexity of doing this in two online sessions with a set of experts with strong and varying opinions. Instead, an adapted SDM approach was utilised. It was initially expected that building a spatial model would require experts to select a from a long list of attributes, however the list of attributes for which spatial data is available was much smaller, constraining the actual decision task. This meant that a discussion around trade-offs was not required in selecting between attributes to create a short-list for modelling. Experts also struggled with the rationale of this SDM application, and some expressed they could not connect the individual attributes to the performance measures quantitatively. An alternative approach was used in a simple ranking of 1-10 scores for each attribute, without building a consequence table assessing each attribute against each performance measure.
Ideally, a pilot study with a test group of participants should have been undertaken.
Followed by several in person meetings, but this was not possible due to the nature of the project and limitations relating to lockdowns associated with Covid 19.
The following benefits and obstacles that arose from the explicit decision-making Workshop 1 -identifying habitat attributes were noted by EM Obstacles:
-Some participants were not fully aware of the purpose of the Workshop and found it hard to engage in a productive manner that stayed on topic.
-There were differing opinions amongst participants and at times those differences created distractions from the topic of interest.
-There were some participants that were outspoken, which took space away from others contributing to the discussions.
-Some participants attended the meeting but did not fill out the follow up questionnaire that ranked the attributes discussed.
-Of the participants who filled out the questionnaire, some only did so for some of the performance criteria and attributes.
Benefits:
-Meeting in an online environment allowed for many people to meet instead of making time and having to travel to a physical destination, which may not have been possible for people living interstate.
-This was the first time a group of experts from several different states had met to discuss habitat attributes associated with BTRW.
-A list of both physical and management attributes was identified and used to inform a Habitat Suitability Model (HSM) for BTRW in both Victoria and the ACT.

In terms of the analysis of attribute ranking, only 10 of the 15 participants filled out the questionnaire. Also, some of the attributes were not ranked against each performance criteria. This means that there could be errors in the distribution of data. For example, there are several outliers in the ranking for rock complexity. Further analysis of this data
shows that this could be due to a mistake when filling out the data sheet, because one participant assigned the same score for all but one performance criteria.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This was the first time a group of experts from several different states met to discuss habitat attributes associated with BTRW. This in itself was a beneficial outcome of the process, since it allowed for networking and sharing of information among a community of practice. Six physical attributes and nine management attributes were identified as important for ongoing BTRW persistence at a site. Feedback from participants was positive and the information and knowledge shared during Workshop 1 was used in the development of a HSM (Chapter 3) and in the development of a ground-truthing protocol (Chapter 4).

Overall, the results from the attribute questionnaires are similar to previous studies that have considered the habitat requirements of BTRW (Tables 1.5, 2.8 & 2.9). An explicit decision-making process was used to rank those habitat attributes in a way that can be applied to a habitat suitability model. Management attributes associated with BTRW have not been identified in any previous studies.

For BTRW populations around Australia, translocations of captive bred individuals to newly established wild populations are a key conservation strategy. The identification of suitable translocation release sites is an important step in implementing this strategy.

Understanding key habitat preferences is paramount in the success of any translocation program. The use of an adapted SDM (Gregory et al., 2012) process to inform the creation of a HSM is an appropriate approach to identify key habitat variables for inclusion in a Habitat Suitability Model for SBTRW in Victoria and ACT and to inform the recommendation of suitable release sites predicted by such a model. The use of an adapted SDM process to aid in the process of identifying model variables, will provide researchers and land managers with more confidence in the final recommendation of potential release locations and lead to greater success for the SBTRW recovery program.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies are known to have a large historical geographical distribution spanning four different states and territories: Queensland (QLD), New South Wales (NSW), Australian Capital Territory (ACT) and Victoria (Menkhorst & Hynes, 2011).

The aim of contemporary habitat suitability modelling is to identify geographical pockets with areas of high habitat suitability within and outside of the current distribution of a species of interest (Guisan & Thuiller, 2005). Such modelling may be used to locate potential translocation sites and focal areas for conservation. Identifying the realised distribution of BTRW, within and outside of the current known range of the species, can be difficult due to the species' cryptic nature and its current sporadic distribution across a vast, remote, and somewhat inaccessible range.

With evolving technology and more accessible data, challenges such as predicting species distributions have been aided by Habitat Suitability Models (HSM). Habitat Suitability Models are used widely by ecologists, policymakers, and conservationists to help identify environmental conditions related to the occurrence of particular species (Guisan & Thuiller, 2005).

Once identified, these environmental conditions -often termed habitat attributes -can be used to identify areas with similar environmental conditions that are currently unoccupied by the species of interest. Such areas can be explored as potential new habitat areas. In summary, HSM correlate observations, such as presence, or presence/absence data with a set of environmental variables to identify areas that provide a similar ecological niche (Elith & Leathwick, 2009;Guisan & Zimmermann, 2000;Hirzel et al., 2006;), thus predicting the potential distribution of the species. Such predictions can be used to identify potential locations for the establishment of new populations of translocated species.

div.head: MaxEnt
div.p: MaxEnt is a publicly available, machine-based Java application, which can use environmental variables and occurrence data to predict a number of different scenarios, such as species distributions, the potential impact of climate change on a species, the emergence of new infectious diseases and the potential for flooding following large rain events (esri, 2023;Phillips et al., 2006Phillips et al., , 2017)). In species distribution models, MaxEnt uses occurrence data and explanatory attribute data based on known locations, to predict an estimate of presence across a study area (esri, 2023). Unlike other HSM that use absence locations, MaxEnt uses presence-only data (esri, 2023;Phillips et al., 2006Phillips et al., , 2017)). Presence data can be derived from direct observations of a species or observations of evidence of that species (e.g. scats and skeletal remains). Such observations are often recorded in publicly available databases of species records (e.g.
in Australia, Atlas of Living Australia and Victorian Biodiversity Atlas).

The potential distribution of a species can be quantified using MaxEnt (Phillips et al., 2021). Species distributions are estimated by finding the "probability distribution of maximum entropy (i.e. closest to uniform) subject to the constraint that the expected value of each environmental variable (or its transform and/or interactions) under this estimated distribution matches its empirical average" (Elith et al., 2006, p.134).

Since becoming available in 2004, MaxEnt has become one of the most successful HSM methods, in terms of its predictive performance, used in determining species distributions in poorly studied landscapes and species, compared with other presenceonly modelling methods (Hernandez et al., 2008).

div.head: Habitat Suitability Modelling and Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies
div.p: Queensland & New South Wales HSM models have previously been used to explore the distribution of BTRW within Australia, but these have been mainly restricted to areas of south-east Qld and northeast NSW (Ashcroft et al., 2014;Morris et al., 2020;Murray et al., 2011;Thurtell et al., 2021). Murray et al. (2011) 2020) used MaxEnt to identify potential translocation sites for BTRW across south-eastern Australia, including areas that were not within the species' known range. Maria Island, located off Tasmania's eastern coast, was identified as having high habitat suitability and is currently fox-free, making it the preferred candidature site in that study (Morris et al., 2020).
