div.head: Current study
div.p: This study is different to Malam (2012) study, because of its use of an adapted Structured Decision Making (SDM) (Gregory et al., 2012) approach at two key stages:
1. to inform the selection of habitat attributes for a HSM, and 2. to inform the recommendation of suitable release sites following modelling.
In addition, this study explores potential suitable habitat for BTRW across the whole of the state of Victoria and in the Australian Capital Territory.

This Chapter describes the use of MaxEnt software to create a HSM to predict potential suitable habitat for the SBTRW in Victoria and the ACT using the habitat attributes identified via the adapted Structured Decision Making (SDM) process described in Chapter 2. While MaxEnt models can sometimes be used to predict the occurrence of populations (Hernandez et al., 2008) of rare species, this study used MaxEnt to predict suitable habitat at which new colonies might be established. This model was used to identify a shortlist of sites across Victoria and the ACT that was later reviewed by a panel of experts using an explicit decision-making process (Chapter 4). After the reviewing process, sites were ground truthed and the accuracy of the model, in terms of its ability to predict suitable habitat was scrutinised (Chapter 4).

div.head: Study area
div.p: The areas of interest for this study are both the state of Victoria and the ACT. Both
Victoria and the ACT are within the former range of SBTRW distribution (Menkhorst & Knight, 2013).

div.head: Victoria
div.p: Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby occurrence data was sourced from the Victorian Biodiversity Atlas (DEECA, 2023) and the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA, 2023) in February 2022. A total of 255 records were extracted from the Victorian Biodiversity Atlas and a total of 270 records from the Atlas of Living Australia. These records comprise physical sightings, scat, and skeletal remains from 1790 -2022. These records were combined, and all duplicate records were removed. Records with a spatial accuracy ≤1000 m were also removed, as

were presence records occurring within 500 m of each other, to reduce spatial autocorrelation (Malam, 2012;Thurtell et al., 2021). This filtered the dataset to a total of 62 spatially valid records suitable for inclusion in the analysis for Victoria.

div.head: Australian Capital Territory
div.p: Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby occurrence data for the ACT was sourced via a data sharing agreement with the ACT Government and from the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA, 2023) in February 2022. A total of 34 records from 1790-2022 were extracted from the ACT Government and the Atlas of Living Australia. As per the Victorian records, all duplicate records were removed and records with a spatial accuracy ≤1000 m were also removed.

Presence records occurring within 500 m of each other were also removed to reduce spatial autocorrelation (Malam, 2012;Thurtell et al., 2021). Although historical records of BTRW within Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve (TNR) were included in the model, all records within the predator proof fences were removed because the higher-than-normal occurrence records found within the area may skew the model output. A BTRW colony which has been supplemented by captive breeding exists within the fenced area at TNR.
These steps filtered the dataset to a total of 21 spatially valid records suitable for inclusion in the analysis for the ACT.

div.head: Habitat and management attributes identified via explicit decision-making Workshop 1 for habitat attributes (Chapter 2)
div.p: Habitat attributes used to model BTRW distribution were based on the results obtained from the Workshop 1 for habitat attributes (Chapter 2). These are summarised in Tables 2.8 and 2.9 (Chapter 2).

div.head: Data preparation
div.p: Four of the six physical attributes identified via Workshop 1 for habitat attributes were used to inform MaxEnt in the modelling process (Table 3.1). Distance to water and vegetation were not used to create the HSM.

Although experts ranked distance to water highly (Chapter 2) it was not included in the model because of the unreliability and sensitivity of the GIS 'water' layers. Vegetation was not used to inform the model, because BTRW are known to consume a wide range of food types (Short, 1989;Van Eeden et al., 2011) and vegetation abundance was considered to have more of an influence rather than vegetation type. Both distance to water and vegetation type were used to filter sites for ground-truthing (Chapter 4). The DEM was used as the elevation layer. Both slope and aspect were derived from the DEM using the tools 'Aspect' and 'Slope' in QGIS. Because QGIS calculates aspect as a circular variable, the aspect layer was converted to a continuous variable ('northeastness') needed for MaxEnt. This was calculated using the 'Raster Calculator' tool using the formulae below.

div.head: 'aspect@1' <= 90 OR 'aspect@1' >=270
div.p: The 'Jackknife' test option was selected to determine the estimated importance of each habitat attribute in the model (Phillips, 2017). The jack-knife test first excludes each variable in turn, and creates a model with the remaining variables (Phillips, 2017). It creates the model using each variable in isolation (Phillips, 2017). All remaining settings were kept as default.

The performance of a MaxEnt model is usually evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) (Phillips, 2017). The AUC is "the estimated probability of the randomly selected grid cell in a correctly adjusted model" (Çoban et al., 2020, pg. 15). If the AUC > 0.5, this indicates the model's performance is better than a random estimation (Elith et al., 2006;Phillips et al., 2015). The closer the AUC is to one, the more sensitive and descriptive the model is considered to be (Çoban et al., 2020;Elith et al., 2006). The average omission rate can also be used to describe the sensitivity and descriptiveness of a model (Phillips, 2017). The closer the test omission rate is to the straight omission rate line, the more sensitive and descriptive the model (Phillips, 2017). Both the AUC, ROC and average omission rates were analysed to determine the performance of the model.

div.head: Victoria
div.p: The average AUC of the ROC across all 15 replicates for the Victorian model is 0.857 (standard deviation 0.069) (Figure 3.1) which means the model is a good fit (Çoban et al., 2020;Gassó et al., 2012). Based on 'percentage contribution', roughness (54.1%) contributed the most to the ACT model; followed by DEM (40.4%), slope (3.3%) and north-eastern aspect (2.2%) (Table 3.3). When evaluated under 'permutation importance', roughness (60.1%) contributed most; followed by DEM (31.8%), north-eastern aspect (6.3%) and slope (1.8%) (Table 3.3). Figure 3.12 shows how each physical attribute affects the MaxEnt prediction for the ACT model. Suitable habitat increased as aspect became more northern (Figure 3.12). As elevation (DEM) increased, so did habitat suitability (Figure 3.12). Optimal elevation was between 459-1300 m above sea level and then slowed as elevation surpassed 1300 m (Figure 3.12). As roughness increased, suitable habitat also increased. Slope had a positive effect on habitat suitability (Figure 3.12). As slope increased, so did habitat suitability with slopes of approximately 15° being most suitable (Figure 3.12).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: This is the first study of its kind to incorporate an explicit decision-making process based on Structured Decision Making (SDM) and Habitat Suitability Modelling (HSM) to model BTRW habitat using MaxEnt software within Victoria and the ACT. By applying the physical attributes identified via the adapted SDM process (Chapter 2) to HSM using MaxEnt software, areas of suitable BTRW habitat were identified in both Victoria and the ACT. The average AUC of the ROC across all 15 replicates for both the Victorian and the ACT models were considered to be of good fit (Figures 3.1 & 3.7) (Çoban et al., 2020;Gassó et al., 2012).

Overall, the two models showed a preference towards rocky and complex (rough) habitat (Tables 3.2 & 3.3). A detailed map showing BTRW habitat suitability was produced from each of the two models. Two areas of high suitability in Victoria were around Gariwerd in western Victoria and locations in eastern Victoria (Figure 3.3). The distribution of high suitability areas predicted by the two models is supported by previous studies both within Victoria and the ACT (Clausen, 2011;Lobert & Waters, 1988a, 1988b;Malam, 2012;Ormay 1996;Waldegrave-Knight, 2002).

The outputs identified in this Chapter are considered further in Chapter 4 which use additional expert elicitation and ground-truthing in conjunction with model outputs to identify the most suitable release sites in Victoria and the ACT for captive bred BTRW.

div.head: Victoria
div.p: The highest percentage contribution to the Victorian model was roughness (67.5%) (Table 3.2). Roughness was used to represent rock complexity because there is currently no spatial data set available measuring rock complexity; and was the physical attribute that scored the highest among BTRW experts (Chapter 2, Tables 2.8 & 2.9). As roughness increased, suitable habitat also increased, with roughness of 5 having optimum suitability (Figure 3.6). Slope (18.7%) was the second highest contributing physical attribute to the Victorian model, followed by DEM (12.9%) and north-eastern aspect (0.9%) (Table 3.2). When evaluated under 'permutation importance', slope (54.2%) contributed most, followed by DEM (28.6%), roughness (15%) and north-eastern aspect
(2.2%) (Table 3.2). Slope had a positive effect on habitat suitability (Figure 3.6). As slope increased, so did habitat suitability, with slopes of approximately 40° being most suitable (Figure 3.6).

As elevation (DEM) increased, so did habitat suitability until it reached 900 m and then habitat suitability decreased (Figure 3.6). Optimal elevation was between 250-900 m above sea level and then decreased as elevation surpassed 900m (Figure 3.6). A study by Carter & Goldizen (2003) suggest that BTRW utilise browsing areas along cliff lines at the tops of escarpments. This may attribute to BTRW preference to higher altitudes, but more research is needed to prove this. Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies (BTRW) show preference to habitats that are steep and highly complex; this may be refection of lower predator numbers (Kinnear et al., 2010;Shelly, 1993;Short & Milkovits, 1990).
Prevalence of the Red Fox (Vulpes vulpes) is lower in areas that consist of steep slopes and elevations between 400 and 1400 m (DELWP, 2021).

The importance of aspect on BTRW habitat suitability has been found to vary in both the literature (Table 1.5) (Chapter 1) and the adapted SDM process results (Table 2.8) (Chapter 2). Aspect contributed only 0.9% to model performance and was not an important contributor to habitat suitability (Table 3.2).

div.head: Australian Capital Territory
div.p: Like the Victorian model, the highest percentage contribution to the ACT model was roughness (54.1%) (Table 3.3). As roughness increased, suitable habitat also increased (Figure 3.12). Elevation (DEM) (40.4%) was the second highest contributing physical attribute to the ACT model, followed by slope (3.3%) and north-eastern aspect (2.2%) (Table 3.3). When evaluated under 'permutation importance', roughness (60.1%) contributed most; followed by DEM (31.8%), north-eastern aspect (6.3%) and slope

As elevation (DEM) increased, so did habitat suitability (Figure 3.12). Optimal elevation was between 459-1300 m above sea level and then slowed as elevation increased from 1300 m (Figure 3.12). These results differ to the Victorian model (Figure 3.6 & 3.12). This could be attributed to the ACT average altitudes being much higher altitude than in Victoria. Areas above the snow line (approximately 1200 m) ranked highly in habitat suitability for the ACT (Figure 3.9). Areas above 1200 m were removed when identifying sites to ground-truth in the ACT, because of the high prevalence of snow in these areas during winter (Chapter 4). Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies have not been historically recorded in areas that have a high prevalence of snowfall and may not be physically equipped to deal with the harsh cold conditions.

Suitable habitat increased as aspect became more northern (Figure 3.12). Slope had a positive effect on habitat suitability (Figure 3.12). As slope increased, so did habitat suitability with slopes of approximately 15° being most suitable (Figure 3.12). Unlike the Victorian model, slope contributed less to the ACT model (Tables 3.2 &3.3).

div.head: Explicit decision-making Workshop 1 for habitat attributes
div.p: The results from Chapter 2 (Workshop 1 for habitat attributes) ranked both physical and management attributes associated with BTRW distribution from most to least important.

The physical attributes identified from the explicit decision-making Workshop 1 for habitat attributes (Chapter 2) and used to produce the models in this Chapter are: roughness (rock complexity), slope, DEM (elevation) and aspect (north-eastern).

Based on the results from this study, roughness (rock complexity) contributed most to BTRW distribution within both Victoria and the ACT. The two models support previous observations suggesting that rock complexity has the greatest influence, above any other habitat attribute, on BTRW distribution across Australia (Lobert & Waters, 1988a, 1988b;Malam, 2012;Morris et al., 2020;Murray et al., 2008Murray et al., , 2011Murray et al., , 2009;;Short, 1982;Waldegrave-Knight, 2002). These results also verify experts' opinions documented in Chapter 2; where rock complexity (roughness) was ranked the most important habitat attribute associated with BTRW distribution (Table 2.8,3.2 & 3.3).

Slope and elevation contributions differed in the Victorian and the ACT models. Slope was the second highest contributor to the Victorian model, followed by elevation. These results coincide with expert opinions from Chapter 2. Elevation was the second highest contributor to the ACT model, followed by slope. Aspect contributed the least to both the Victorian and ACT models. Aspect was ranked as having the least importance from expert opinions in Chapter 2.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: A common issue faced by many researchers when using Habitat Suitability Models (HSM) to predict species distributions is access to appropriate spatial data sets (Eyre, 2018;Eyre et al., 2022). Data sets may not contain the detail needed to predict a species distribution for fine-scale, site level attributes (Eyre, 2018;Eyre et al., 2022). Habitat attributes such as rock complexity can be assessed on a large-scale using Light Detection and Ranging (LIDAR) (Acebes et al., 2021) but these data sets are often cost-prohibitive to obtain (Eyre 2018;Eyre et al. 2022).

Occurrence records that cannot be spatially verified pose the risk of distorting a species' association with known habitat attributes (Naimi et al., 2014). In this study, this was avoided by removing occurrence records with poor spatial verification.

It can be risky when predicting the distribution of a species into novel environments, because species occurrence data is not available to directly support predictions (Elith & Leathwick, 2009). Presence-only records are often subject to sampling bias because data 123 can be collected haphazardly (Elith et al., 2006;Yackulic et al., 2013), therefore datasets require filtering to increase model performance (Boria et al., 2014). In this study presence records occurring within 500 m of each other were removed to reduce spatial autocorrelation (Malam, 2012;Thurtell et al., 2021).

Unlike similar studies by Thurtell ( 2022) and Thurtell et al. (2021) this study did not create separate bias files. A bias file helps avoid sampling habitat outside of a species' known occurrence or can account for collection sampling biases with coordinate data (Brown, 2017). The two models described in this Chapter did not include bias files because extensive search efforts have been conducted for BTRW in Victoria and the ACT (Lobert & Waters 1988a, 1988b;Ormay, 1996). Ground-truthing modelled sites is necessary to evaluate and validate the model's predictions. This will be further explored in Chapter 4.

Although considered in Chapter 4, the two HSM for Victoria and the ACT may have been limited by not including the management attributes identified in Chapter 2 (Table 2.9), such as predation risk, into the models. Lack of effective control of predator and competitor species, may cause species such as BTRW to utilise habitat that serves as survival refugia, instead of their preferred habitat (Kinnear et al., 2010;Ruykys, 2011).

Given ongoing predation risks and competition for resources (Table 1.3), further investigation is required into the refugial associations of BTRW, rather than habitat preferences (Kinnear et al., 2010;Ruykys, 2011).

MaxEnt outperforms other HSM with regard to predictive accuracy and ease of use (Merow et al., 2013). In this study, default settings for MaxEnt were used, and the performance of the model was determined using the standard approach, which is the area under the curve (AUC) of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and average omission rates. Expert elicitation and ground-truthing were used to further validate the model, overcoming some of the criticisms (Liu et al., 2011;Merow et al., 2013), that AUC values overinflate the accuracy of the model.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Habitat Suitability Models (HSM) have proven to be effective tools for evaluating the potential distribution of species and to inform conservation decisions (Da Silva Neto et al., 2020;Guisan et al., 2013). A review by Guisan et al., 2013 suggests the use of HSM is recommended to support conservation decision making. However, evidence supporting HSM as a solution for on-ground conservation problems remains scarce in the published literature (Da Silva Neto et al., 2020;Guisan et al., 2013;Sánchez-Mercado et al., 2018).

A review by Fois et al. (2018) found the use of methods to enhance habitat suitability modelling (HSM) is increasing in the published literature. Such methods address concerns (e.g. Greaves et al., 2006) that studies using HSM can lack critical evaluation of model performance. Some of the methods used to enhance HSM outputs and to evaluate the performance of a model include: selection of appropriate environmental attributes and their application within a HSM (Bucklin et al., 2015), and consideration of sample size and data quality for presence data (e.g. Bloom et al., 2018;Fois et al., 2018;Hernandez et al., 2006;van Proosdij et al., 2016).

Habitat suitability models, particularly MaxEnt models, assume that species occurrence data can be used to typify areas best suited to the species of interest, and can therefore be used to identify locations with suitable habitat for past, present or future populations locations (Sánchez-Mercado et al., 2018). The models do this by identifying areas which have high probability of suitability and in some instances, on-ground investigations can show that predictions are inaccurate. In such cases, ground-truthing shows that the species of interest and/or their required habitat attributes are not found in areas that are ranked highly by the models (Sánchez-Mercado et al., 2018).

The disparity between modelled outputs and actual scenarios may reflect inaccuracies within the HSM itself (Sánchez-Mercado et al., 2018). Such disparities may be caused by errors involving attribute selection, and/or the use of outdated or incorrect occurrence data (Sánchez-Mercado et al., 2018).

To have confidence in any HSM, it is necessary to validate the model. Validation can be achieved statistically and/or by verifying the model under real-world conditions. There are several statistical methods used to validate HSM (Greaves et al., 2006). Most of these methods involve comparing output from the model with subsets of the training data (Greaves et al., 2006). For example, the most common method used to measure the capability of a HSM to make accurate predictions of habitat suitability is to consider the area under the receiving operating characteristic curve (known as AUC) (Elith et al., 2010).

The AUC is a standard measure of predictive model performance. It can be defined as the area under a plot of the proportion of true positives versus the proportion of false positives; a value of 0.5 indicates a model with no discriminatory power, and a value of 1 indicates a model that correctly identifies all records (Bowden et al., 2021). The AUC is simple to use and very easy to interpret, hence its popularity among researchers (Anderson, 2016).

Despite its widespread use, this method of HSM validation has received considerable criticism (Anderson, 2016;Lobo et al., 2008). The AUC puts a weighted error on both commission (presence) and omission (absence) equally, and does not provide information on the spatial distribution of model errors (Anderson, 2016;Lobo et al., 2008).

Validation of a HSM can also be achieved by comparing its output with real-world situations, and/or by conferring with experts within a given field (e.g Eyre et al., 2022;Ferrier et al., 2002). Experts can be used to discern whether model outputs are logical, and their specific field knowledge can also be used to prioritise and rank sites identified by the model (Eyre et al., 2022). In studies which use HSM to inform conservation decisions, experts are likely to be conservation practitioners with detailed local knowledge of the study area and/or of the species of interest. Methods where experts are asked to validate models can be delivered within the adapted framework of Structured Decision Making (SDM). This method of collating expert opinion is similar to the method of expert elicitation used in this study to select habitat attributes to be included as inputs to the model (Chapter 3).

Applying an adapted Structured Decision Making (SDM) (Gregory et al. 2012) process to review HSM output is a step rarely taken (Guisan et al., 2013). However, a recent study by Eyre et al. (2022) combined HSM with expert recommendations, to select a subset of areas within Victoria from a wider group of areas predicted by a HSM model to contain suitable habitat for the critically endangered Leadbeater's Possum (Gymnobelideus leadbeateri). This study also used an adapted SDM style process to prioritise 80 sites for camera trap surveys and led to the detection of Leadbeater's Possum at a location for which no previous records existed (Eyre et al., 2022).

A review by Guisan et al. (2013Guisan et al. ( , p. 1425) ) found that the "bulk of peer-reviewed literature clearly lacks the perspective of practitioners and decision makers on how HSM can contribute to solving environmental problems, despite HSM construction often being justified based on their potential utility for decision making". There are many tools published in the literature, but little advice suggested to support decision making processes regarding conservation objectives (Guisan et al., 2013). Guisan et al. (2013) suggest that for HSM to be constructed in a more appropriate manner that can be used to guide conservation actions, there needs to be a better understanding of the decision process on the part of researchers. Decision makers need to also provide feedback to researchers, regarding their conservation objectives and the use of HSM (Guisan et al., 2013).

Due to the aforementioned criticism surrounding purely statistical validation of HSM (Anderson, 2016;Lobo et al., 2008), ground-truthing of HSM output is often recommended (Greaves et al., 2006;Sánchez-Mercado et al., 2018). Ground-truthing involves undertaking field-based surveys in order to validate the predictions of a HSM.

Ground-truthing can be used to support or negate HSM output by assessing real world scenarios. The study on Leadbeater's Possum (Eyre et al., 2022) highlighted the paucity of studies which combine HSM with ground-truthing surveys. More often than not, ground-truthing of predicted sites is not conducted due to time and cost constraints (Da Silva Neto et al., 2020;Greaves et al., 2006;Thurtell et al., 2021).

Because ground-truthing can be expensive and time consuming, it is important to prioritise candidate sites with most promise for ground-truthing; and this task can be undertaken by experts. Eyre et al. (2022) noted that those studies which use groundtruthing techniques to validate HSM have generally not utilised the process of expert elicitation. The validation of HSM output through both expert elicitation and groundtruthing results in a model output that can be used more confidently to inform conservation-based decisions (Eyre et al., 2022).

The aim of this Chapter is to use an adapted SDM process to critically evaluate and refine the output of the two HSM described in Chapter 3 to confidently identify sites in Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) which may be suitable for the establishment of new BTRW colonies. After the model outputs were evaluated and refined by a group of experts, ground-truthing of sites considered most likely to be suitable for the establishment of new BTRW colonies was undertaken. A final list of candidate sites was produced to inform the SBTRW Recovery Team about suitable BTRW translocation sites in Victoria and the ACT.
The Chapter is structured so that methods and results for the explicit decision-making activities are reported first, followed by the methods and results for ground truthing.

The purpose of the explicit decision-making activities described in this Chapter was to identify which of the sites predicted by the MaxEnt model (Chapter 3) were most likely to be suitable for the establishment of new BTRW colonies and therefore prioritised for ground-truthing. The explicit decision-making activities involved discussions at a Workshop followed by independent ranking of sites by experts, using a "traffic light criteria system" described below. The explicit decision-making activities resulted in the identification of a subset of sites for ground-truthing. The final output of this Chapter is the list of candidate sites presented to the SBTRW Recovery Team.

div.head: -Ranking candidate release sites for ground-truthing using an explicit decision-making process
1. 1 -Methods
div.p: The work presented in this Chapter, and in Chapter 2, was undertaken with the approval of the Federation University Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC approval: B21-142). The starting point for the work described in this Chapter was the HSM model output from Chapter 3.

An invitation, explanatory statement and consent forms to participate in the explicit decision-making activities described in this Chapter was sent to the invitees for Workshop 1 (Chapter 2) (HERE). Methods for the identification and invitation of these individuals are provided in Chapter 2. The explicit decision-making activities for this Chapter included a second Workshop, during which experts considered the HSM output, followed by an exercise in which all experts were asked to work independently to rank sites within three geographical areas (that we termed 'complexes') identified during the Workshop. Twenty participants were invited to participate in Workshop 2 for site selection, and 11 attended. Ten participants subsequently participated in the independent ranking task that followed the workshop; two of these focussed on the Gariwerd complex, five on the Little River Gorge complex and three on the ACT complex.

div.head: Habitat Suitability Model output
div.p: A map booklet document (available HERE) was produced to inform the participants of Workshop 2 for site selection about the model outputs. The booklet presented the model outputs from the Habitat Suitability Model (HSM) as a series of maps, produced in QGIS (QGIS 2022). The criteria surrounding this map booklet was developed and discussed with the supervisory team. 'Areas', 'clusters' and 'candidate sites' were established.
The maps showed, for both Victoria and the ACT:
-Locations identified by the model as having suitable habitat for BTRW -Historical BTRW records -Land tenure -Geographical areas delineated to allow targeted discussions

The map booklet included instructions to participants about how to use their expert knowledge to rank geographical areas and sites identified by the model in terms of their suitability for BTRW. To facilitate discussion and to allow the experts to focus on areas and locations, a series of nested geographical categories were identified and transposed onto the mapped HSM output (Figure 4.3).

• 'Areas' were the largest of these and were defined as large (up to 50,000 ha) areas within Victoria and the ACT. There were 28 'Areas' defined in Victoria (Figure 4.1), and four 'Areas' defined in ACT (Figure 4.2).
• 'Clusters' of sites were to be identified by experts during Workshop 2.

Clusters comprised groups of modelled potential BTRW release sites within each area. It was originally intended that experts would consider sites by cluster in order to prioritise sites for ground truthing, based on the management attributes identified in Workshop 1 (Chapter 2). Clusters typically encompassed around 5000 ha.

• 'Candidate sites' were sites, within each cluster, that were to be identified by experts during Workshop 2 after considering the management attributes identified in Workshop 2 (Chapter 2). Candidate sites were typically larger than 15 ha in size.
The 'Land Tenure' QGIS layer was used as a filter to remove candidate sites on private land.

div.p: Explicit decision-making Workshop 2 was a half-day meeting held on the 1 st of July 2022 via Microsoft Teams. Workshop participants reported that the map booklets did not provide sufficient information to allow them to comment on the suitability of areas and clusters for the establishment of new BTRW colonies. Experts also indicated that they were not comfortable to comment on geographical areas with which they were not familiar. Experts suggested that the area scale was too large to allow meaningful comment. It was therefore necessary to introduce an additional step, in which the Workshop participants were provided with a summary of the outcomes from Workshop 2, plus some additional information, and were then asked to independently rank 'individual candidate sites' in terms of their potential to contain suitable BTRW habitat, and therefore to focus ground truthing efforts. Details are provided below.

An important outcome of Workshop 2 was the identification of three broad geographic areas which most experts agreed had the most potential for the establishment of new BTRW colonies. These were: the ACT, Gariwerd (Victoria) and East Gippsland (Victoria).

Changes were made to the methodology described in the original map booklet and three new modified map booklet documents were created (These three booklets are available HERE). The modified booklets disregarded the concepts of areas and clusters and instead grouped potential BTRW release sites, identified by the MaxEnt model, into larger geographical regions named complexes. The booklets described three complexes which varied in size. These were the ACT complex, the Gariwerd complex and the Little River Gorge complex.

The ACT complex covered the whole of the Australian Capital Territory (approximately 235,800 hectares) whereas the Gariwerd (Grampians) complex only contained areas of the National Park and the neighbouring Black Range State Park (approximately 76,898 hectares). The Little River Gorge complex focussed on an area in East Gippsland, Victoria of approximately 81,658 hectares).

div.head: Traffic light criteria system
div.p: Using the outcomes from Workshop 2 for site selection, a traffic light criteria system was developed to help the experts prioritise sites for ground-truthing (Table 4.2). This traffic light criteria system was developed with the help of both the supervisory and advisory teams.
The traffic light criteria system was employed in two steps:

1. The researcher identified broad geographic areas (complexes), and potential BTRW release sites within each complex, from HDM output. The researcher then classified each potential BTRW release site within each of the three complexes as red, yellow, or green. Sites classified by the researcher as red were proposed to be unsuitable for SBTRW colony establishment, and therefore not prioritised for ground-truthing. Sites classified as green were proposed to be highly suitable for BTRW colony establishment and therefore high priority for ground-truthing. Sites classified as yellow were proposed to have some potential for SBTRW colony establishment.
2. Experts reviewed the classification completed by the researcher and, using their local geographical knowledge, ranked sites for ground-truthing.

In developing the traffic light criteria system, the researcher focused on the three broad geographical regions (termed complexes) identified by participants in Workshop 2 as most likely to contain habitat suitable for the establishment of new BTRW release sites.

The modified map booklets were accompanied by written instructions for the use of a 'traffic light ranking system', developed to enable the experts to consider and rank candidate sites independently, as to which were best suited as potential BTRW release sites. The modified map booklets included an overview of each of the three complexes, and descriptive detailed information on each site within each complex. The documents identified and described a total of 224 potential BTRW release sites. div.head: Ground-truthing protocol
div.p: Parks Victoria and ACT National Parks and Wildlife Services were notified before field work commenced. Park staff assisted in accessing some sites and provided gate keys to areas that were not accessible to the public. They also provided information on road closures and alternative access routes where relevant.

Prior to ground-truthing sites identified by experts during the independent ranking exercise, a ground-truthing protocol was developed and trialled in Lerderderg State Park, Victoria. It became apparent during the pilot study that this ground-truthing protocol was too detailed and was better suited for site evaluations immediately preceding a translocation, instead of a rapid verification of the HSM output coupled with expert advice about site suitability. For example, the original protocol required detailed data collection regarding the number of, and width(s) of, cave entrances at each site, along with photographs of each habitat element. These requirements would have resulted in a considerable time commitment at each site to complete ground-truthing, ultimately not being conducive to a rapid assessment.

Modified aspects of the methodology of Gaborov and Corrigan (2019) A data sheet for the ground-truthing protocol was developed for use in the Proof Safe app (Proof Safe, 2022). Proof Safe is a commercially available application that creates custom data forms for any project (Proof Safe, 2022). Available for Android or iOS devices, Proof Safe allows field data to be recorded consistently and stored safely. It can be used where there is little to no phone reception. Once the device is returned to an area with coverage, the data is securely uploaded to a central database (Proof Safe, 2022). Both physical and digital ground-truthing assessment sheets were used in the field (Appendix 5).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: This Chapter demonstrates the advantages of combining HSM and ground-truthing methods with an adapted SDM approach to inform the selection of potential BTRW translocation sites within Victoria and the ACT. In this study, the output of the HSM described in Chapter 3 was refined by consulting experts during SDM processes, and then further refined by ground-truthing.

div.head: Ranking candidate release sites for ground-truthing using an adapted
Structured Decision Making process
div.p: As was the case for the work described in Chapter 2, the adapted SDM processes presented in this Chapter experienced both challenges and beneficial outcomes.

The initial purpose of Workshop 2 for site selection was to identify clusters of sites, from the HSM output, that were considered most likely to be able to support future BTRW colonies within Victoria and the ACT. As experts voiced their opinions it became apparent that this outcome could not be achieved during the Workshop. The original map booklets did not provide adequate material to allow experts to comment on the suitability of areas and clusters for the establishment of new BTRW colonies.

Experts also indicated that they would prefer to comment only on the suitability of potential release sites within geographical regions with which they were familiar. The group suggested a more targeted approach that maximised their local knowledge.

An important outcome of Workshop 2 was the identification of three broad geographic areas which most experts agreed had the most potential for the establishment of new BTRW colonies. These were: the ACT, Gariwerd (Victoria) and East Gippsland (Victoria).
This outcome shaped the remaining work in the study.

div.head: Traffic light system
div.p: While the original intention for Workshop 2 for site selection was not met, experts contributed valuable insights and knowledge to discussions and answered several of the original questions posed during the Workshop. These discussions and answers were used to inform the development of the traffic light criteria system and facilitated the independent ranking activity undertaken after the Workshop.

The use of a 10 metre Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to create the attributes: slope, aspect and roughness in Victoria may have resulted in slightly inaccurate model predictions. Currently there is no GIS tool or layer that specifically represents rock complexity. In this study, the amount of irregularity of the surface derived from a DEM was used to indicate roughness. This was calculated using the largest inter-cell difference of a central pixel and its surrounding cell (QGIS, 2022) and may have created inaccuracies.

Another explanation for inaccurate predictions could be due to the (>0. 85-1.0) filter applied to the MaxEnt model output raster value. Increasing the value extent to greater than 0.85 may have resulted in habitat better suited for BTRW.
These slight discrepancies between model output and real-world conditions highlight the importance of ground-truthing and physically validating sites.

div.head: Highly suitable sites
div.p: Following ground-truthing, two of the 19 sites were identified as being highly suitable for the establishment of new BTRW colonies, and these were both in Victoria: Little River Gorge site 15 and Gariwerd site 13 ( Gorge sites 14 and 16, which were observed from site 15 and considered to have homogenous habitat (Table 4.9) provided an ideal release site for captive bred BTRW (Tables 4.10 & 4.14). Field notes describe the site as having "the best and most extensive rock in East Gippsland". Many areas within this site are inaccessible to humans, and additional investigation with drones could be beneficial.
Ground-truthing at Gariwerd site 13 recorded an abundance of boulders, caves and ledges, over-hangs, and rock piles throughout the site (Table 4.11 and Figure 4.10).
There were no signs of predators and access within the site is steep in parts (Table 4.11).

Predator species may have access to the site, especially in the grazing areas, but would likely struggle to access boulder piles (Table 4.11). The boundary of the site is also relatively easily accessible from Asses Ears Road which has advantages for logistics associated with translocation operations.

A single BTRW colony currently exists at Gariwerd, located at Moora Moora, approximately 16 kilometres in a direct line from site 13 (Figure 4.15). The Moora Moora colony was established between 2008 and 2012, using captive bred individuals. This occurred after the last known wild BTRW was removed from Gariwerd and placed in captivity in 1999 (Taggart et al., 2015). A total of 39 BTRW were translocated to the Moora Moora site during 2008-2012 (Taggart et al., 2015).

Although Moora Moora was one of two translocation sites that ranked highly for BTRW suitability in a study by Taggart et al., (2008), this site has since been considered unsuitable for BTRW translocations, due to the limited success and recruitment of the colony (Coulson, 2019). Neither the HSM in the current study, nor in a study by Malam (2012), identified the Moora Moora site as appropriate for BTRW translocations. Because foxes have been recorded to travel 16 km in a night (Carter et al., 2012), it is possible that a fox could consume a BTRW at or near the Moora Moora site and travel to these areas. However, it is also plausible that an extant BTRW population currently exists, or recently existed, in this area. Examination and identification of the recently discovered skeletal remains and faecal material and targeted surveys of the area are necessary to confirm this hypothesis. If evidence of recent or current BTRW occupation is found, this may further confirm the suitability of Gariwerd site 13 as a release site for captive bred BTRW. Given the similarity of Gariwerd site 14, this site is also recommended as a potential release site for BTRW.

div.head: Suitable sites
div.p: Six sites; three in the Little River Gorge complex (13, 28 & 29), two in Gariwerd (1 and 19) and one in the ACT (site 37) were identified as being suitable ( Little River Gorge site 13 was assessed as suitable to support BTRW. This site contains enough complex rock, but there was concern that the site itself may not be large enough to support enough individuals to establish a viable colony (Table 4.10). This site may not be appropriate as a release site but may be utilised by individuals moving through the landscape (Table 4.10).
Australian Capital Territory site 37 is considered capable of supporting a small colony.

This site contains the appropriate physical attributes such as boulder piles, caves, overhangs, ledges, and vegetation (Table 4.12). This site is just above 1200m (snowline) (Table 4.12), which may be of some concern for translocations in the near future because BTRW have not been historically recorded in areas that have a high prevalence of snowfall and may not be physically equipped to deal with the harsh cold conditions (Ashcroft et al., 2014); but with future average temperatures predicted to rise due to climate change, this concern may be ameliorated.

There was also evidence of pig occupancy close to this site, which could cause habitat degradation and competition to BTRW. Evidence of Lyrebird diggings were also apparent, which could suggest lower predation pressure within this site.
ACT site 37 was the only site recommended for BTRW translocations in the ACT but may not be the most appropriate considering many sites were not ground-truthed.

and showed characteristics homogenous with site 19, which runs along the same ridgeline and links to site 19. Gariwerd site 22 includes the area occupied by the last remaining wild BTRW (Taggart et al., 2015). This individual was removed in 1999 (Taggart et al., 2015). Assessments of sites 20 and 22 should also be carried out to establish whether these sites have the potential to sustain future BTRW colonies. If so, this area could be ideal for future BTRW translocations in Gariwerd because of the connectivity among these sites.

Gariwerd site 14 was not assessed but was considered homogenous with Gariwerd site 13 (Table 4.9). Sites 14 was observed from a distance and showed similar characteristics to site 13. This site did not run along the same ridge line as site 13 but did run adjacent.

No verified historical records of BTRW presence have been collected from Gariwerd site 13, although there are unverified BTRW scat records from the Asses Ears area, which is in the same vicinity (Malam, 2012). A study by Malam (2012) used these unverified BTRW scat records to generate an HSM. Many of these occurrence records have not been verified and were not used to inform the HSM used in this study. A review of these records is needed, to create a more comprehensive list of BTRW occurrences. This will allow for better HSM in the future.

It is also worth considering the areas along the Glenelg River Road in Gariwerd, where BTRW remains were confirmed in fox scat (Sinclair, 2020). There were no sites identified for ground-truthing nearby, but areas that contain high habitat suitability may be worth further investigation.

div.head: Australian Capital Territory
div.p: Attempts were made to assess sites 12, 13 and 14 in the ACT, but access to these sites was deemed too difficult within the time constraints and resources of this study (Table 4.13). These sites are along Cow Flat Creek, a tributary of the Cotter River that flows into the Bendora Dam within the Cotter River Catchment (Table 4.13). This is the source of the ACT's drinking water supply (Table 4.13). Vegetation was extremely thick at these sites, which hindered access (Table 4.13). Access attempts were also made along Cow Flat Creek, but the creek was too deep to cross due to recent rains. Cow Flat Creek appears to be the most direct route to access these sites, but waders and/or a change of clothes and footwear are needed to access the sites safely and comfortably. Further exploration of these sites is recommended.

ACT sites 22 and 63 were previously assessed by staff from TNR and Wildlife Unlimited (Table 4.13). The notes from these previous assessments indicate that these sites have potential as future BTRW translocation sites, especially site 22, which was described as an area of high habitat complexity and suitability (Table 4.13). However, access to site 22 is only possible by boat (Table 4.13), which adds complexity to translocation logistics.
ACT site 61 has been identified by TNR staff as a prospective site for future BTRW translocations, prior to this study and has excellent accessibility (Table 4.13).
Attempts were made to assess sites 1, 2 and 59, but due to road closures, these sites were unable to be accessed (Table 4.9).
It would be useful to visit and assess these eight ACT sites (1, 2, 12, 13, 14, 22, 59 and 63) to apply the ground-truthing protocol used in this study.

div.head: Other considerations
div.p: Because of the nature of the terrain with which BTRW are associated, it was not possible to ground-truth every site predicted by the HSM as suitable for BTRW. The application of the traffic light criteria system was useful to filter sites by management attributes such as terrain difficulty, distance from roads/walking track/access points and land tenure.
This filtering resulted in the exclusion of some areas that ranked highly in the HSM when prioritising sites for ground-truthing.
Areas such as Rocky Plains Creek, which falls within the Little River Gorge complex was not listed as a site in this study because it did not fall within the traffic light criteria;

being more than 2kms from the nearest access point. This area was an extant site up until the 1990's. The last known BTRW occurrence was at the bottom of the Rocky Plains Creek catchment, but most of the upper catchment remains unsurveyed. There were no sites identified for ground-truthing nearby using the traffic light system criteria, but there were areas that contain high habitat suitability nearby and may be worth further investigation.
It may be worth considering other areas that ranked highly within the Victorian model but were eliminated by experts in the second Workshop 2 for site selection.
For example:
• Langi Ghiran/Mount Cole areas
• Pyrenees State Forest area

div.head: • Areas along the Macalister River
div.p: There are no past verified BTRW records within these areas identified above, and although these areas ranked highly, there are higher risks and potential environmental concerns associated with assisted migration translocations, over translocations into a species known range (Seddon et al., 2009). Past translocations of the BTRW, into Hawaii (Eldridge & Browning 2002;Lazell et al., 1984) and New Zealand (Eldridge et al., 2001) are good examples of the potential consequences BTRW can have on other species and the environment when moving BTRW outside their home range.

Although predation and competitor species observations were recorded in the groundtruthing process, further assessments prior to translocations of both highly suitable and suitable sites is still needed to ensure numbers can be easily managed/controlled/eradicated.

More research is needed into the importance of water and its influence on BTRW habitat suitability. Distance to water scored second to rock complexity in Workshop 1 for habitat attributes, but when discussed in Workshop 2 for site selection, there were differences in opinions regarding the importance of distance to water. It may be worth considering, rainfall instead of distance to water, but that as an attribute it is hard to measure because of its disparity within a landscape.

The use of different technologies, such as drones and Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) may be a more cost-effective method in the long run, that could allow for a broader range of areas to be assessed in greater detail and in a timelier fashion. These methods also allow for areas that cannot be accessed by humans on foot, to be surveyed and assessed. LiDAR may also provide the HSM with a more exact representation of what's really on ground and avoid issues such as incorrect habitat suitability.

There have previously been two studies modelling habitat suitability of BTRW using MaxEnt in Victoria (Malam, 2012;Morris et al., 2020). The study by Morris et al. (2020) differs from the current study because the model output is at a much broader scale. Morris et al. (2020) predicts a vast area of Eastern Australia -from Queensland to Tasmania, as having suitable BTRW habitat. Some of the model outputs from the study by Malam (2012), which does not provide finer scale predictions do align with the output in this thesis, but Malam's (2012) study is limited to Gariwerd and does not extend to other areas of Victoria or the ACT.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Using an adapted SDM process at two key stages to inform 1: selection of key physical and management attributes to be used in a HSM (Chapter 2) and 2: to prioritise sites, within experts' local knowledge areas, for ground-truthing (Chapter 4), has proved to be an effective method to identify potential BTRW release sites and direct ground-truthing efforts across an extensive geographic region. This study contributes to existing knowledge and literature and has filled significant gaps in the knowledge of site selection in BTRW translocations in both Victoria and the ACT.
These results are extremely promising and will be used by the SBTRW Recovery Team to inform future BTRW translocations.

div.head: Chapter 5 : Final recommendations and conclusion
div.p: This study has demonstrated the advantages of combining an adapted Structured Decision Making (SDM) process, habitat suitability modelling (HSM) and ground-truthing methods to inform potential Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby (BTRW) translocation sites within

Victoria and the ACT. Previous studies (e.g. Malam, 2012;Morris et al., 2020;Thurtell, 2022;Thurtell et al., 2021) have all used HSM, in particular MaxEnt modelling to predict suitable BTRW habitat across Australia. Malam (2012) is the first to have identified Wales Although this study is not the first of its kind to use HSM to predict BTRW habitat suitability, it is the first of its kind to apply an explicit decision-making process adapted from SDM (Gregory et al., 2012) at two key stages. By combining HSM and an adapted SDM process, this study has been able to identify suitable and highly suitable habitat for BTRW across Victoria and the ACT. The use of an adapted SDM process and groundtruthing methods to validate the model outputs and prioritise sites for ground-truthing has ensured that the final ranking of potential candidate sites can be reliably used by the SBTRW Recovery Team to inform future translocations.
More ground-truthing of sites is needed in both Victoria, but particularly in the ACT, where only two sites were ground-truthed.

Although not ground-truthed in this study, the sites identified in Table 4.16 should be investigated further. These sites have been identified via previous on-ground assessments and expert opinions (Table 4.16).

While the scope of this project was not to identify areas that could potentially contain extant BTRW colonies, it may be worth investigating areas that ranked highly in the HSM within Gariwerd. Combining the results from this study, the potential BTRW remains found at Gariwerd complex site 13 and the fox scats from Sinclair's (2020) study, it may help direct land managers to new unidentified BTRW colonies within Gariwerd. It is worth assessing in greater detail the areas surrounding site 13 and highly ranked areas along the Glenelg River Road that are in close proximity to the fox scat remains identified in Sinclair's (2020) study.

div.head: Captive breeding
div.p: There are currently several captive breeding programs for BTRW across Australia, promoting genetic diversity and ensuring the security of the species. These include programs located at:
• Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve (TNR), Paddy's River, Australian Capital Territory (SESU)
• Mount Rothwell Conservation and Research Reserve, Little River, Wyndham, Victoria (SESU)
• Waterfall Springs Wildlife Sanctuary, Kulnura, New South Wales (Hybrid SESU & CESU)
• Taronga Conservation Society Australia, Taronga, New South Wales (CESU)

Both Mt Rothwell Conservation and Research Reserve and Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve (TNR) house captive populations of SBTRW that have been a source for past and future translocations in both Victoria and the ACT. More than 130 individuals comprise the SBTRW captive breeding program at Mt Rothwell and TNR (Hill, 2022). Both of these captive breeding programs are considered successful, with the recent creation of two new predator-proof fenced enclosures within Victoria's Strathbogie Ranges (Widgewah Sanctuary) and an additional safe haven at TNR in the ACT. These enclosures will house additional SBTRW colonies and will be used for both conservation and translocation purposes.

div.head: Habitat suitability of the Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby
div.p: It is essential that the habitat requirements of BTRW are well understood and incorporated into site selection processes associated with reintroductions, reinforcements, and assisted colonisation (Appendix 1). Coulson (2019, p. 8) states that "habitat is a multidimensional entity, so an analytical, rather than descriptive, approach is required to integrate all the elements potentially comprising suitable habitat".

Important features of the habitat that support the presence of BTRW can be included in Habitat Suitability Models as habitat attributes. These include characteristics of the habitat at broad (landscape) and local (site) scales. There have been several studies across Australia examining and modelling habitat quality and suitability for the BTRW Chapter 2 : Identification of key habitat attributes for the Brush-tailed Rockwallaby in Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory using an explicit decisionmaking process
Chapter 3 : Modelling potential release sites for Brush-tailed Rock-wallabies in Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory.

Separate HSM models were created for Victoria and the ACT because of the differences in the Digital Elevation Model (DEM) between the state and territory (Table 3.1). QGIS 3.28 (QGIS, 2022) was used for all geoprocessing. Prior to spatial analysis, all spatial data (for both Victoria and the ACT) was converted to EPSG: 4283 (GDA94) using the 'Reproject' tool in QGIS. All data layers were resampled to have the same cell size (ACT = 0.0002777777779999999748 and VIC = 0.0001054858249999999939) and extents (ACT = 148.7629166675160093, -35.1245833317649954 and VIC = 140.8662358313640084, -35.8640079862940055). MaxEnt requires raster files to be converted to ASC files (Phillips et al., 2017). Raster files were converted to ASC files using the 'Translate (Convert Format)' tool in QGIS. Table 3.1 describes each attribute and source used to inform the two different models.

Currently, there are no GIS data layers measuring rock complexity. Instead, 'roughness' was derived from the DEM using the 'Roughness' tool. Roughness is the amount of irregularity of the surface derived from a DEM. It is calculated by "using the largest intercell difference of a central pixel and its surrounding cell" (QGIS, 2022). Effectively, this was considered a suitable surrogate measure for rock complexity.

div.head: MaxEnt settings
div.p: MaxEnt version 3.4 was used to create the HSM (Phillips et al., 2021). Digital Elevation Model (DEM) (elevation), slope, north-eastern aspect, and roughness (rock complexity)
were the continuous attributes used to create the HSM.

Fifteen 'cross validate' replicates were used to train the model. Cross validation is a "form of replication where the occurrence data is randomly split into several equal-size groups called 'folds', and models are created leaving out each fold in turn. The left-out folds are then used for evaluation" (Phillips, 2017, p. 24). The cross-validation replication method is better for smaller data sets because it uses all of the data to train the model (Phillips, 2017). To prevent MaxEnt from over-predicting and/or under-predicting attribute relationships, 'maximum iterations' were set at 5,000 to allow for greater model convergence (Young et al., 2011). To reduce disk space and to speed up the analysis process, the 'write clamp grid' and 'write output grid' options were turned off (Phillips, 2017;Young et al., 2011). The 'Max number of background points' was set to 10,000. Based on 'percentage contribution', roughness (67.5%) contributed the most to the Victorian model; followed by slope (18.7%), DEM (12.9%) and north-eastern aspect (0.9%) (Table 3.2). When evaluated under 'permutation importance', slope (54.2%) contributed most; followed by DEM (28.6%), roughness (15%) and north-eastern aspect (2.2%) (Table 3.2).

div.p: The average AUC of the ROC across all 15 replicates for the ACT model is 0.768 (standard deviation 0.180) (Figure 3.7) which means the model is a good fit (Çoban et al., 2020;Gassó et al., 2012).

div.head: 1. 2 -Results for the explicit decision-making Workshop 2 for site selection
div.p: While the original intention for Workshop 2 for site selection was not met (participants were not able to identify a short list of sites for ground-truthing during the Workshop), the discussions held during the Workshop, including the answers (Table 4.3) to the questions posed during the Workshop, informed the development of the traffic light criteria system and facilitated the ranking activity undertaken subsequent to the Workshop.

In general, EM undertook ground-truthing. An exception was for the East Gippsland sites, where staff of Wildlife Unlimited Pty. Ltd. were contracted to undertake groundtruthing These staff worked under the direction of EM and used the same groundtruthing protocol. They also recorded their results via the Proof Safe app.

Prior to fieldwork, maps of sites to be ground-truthed were produced using QGIS (QGIS, 2022) and imported into Avenza Maps (Avenza 2023) phone application. Avenza (Avenza, 2023) and a Garmin GPSMAP 64csx GPS were used to log tracks, record way points and store images at each site. Photographs and videos taken during groundtruthing were also recorded, as well as any other additional information.

Once ground-truthing of sites concluded, the data from the surveyed sites were reviewed and collated. Ground-truthed sites were assigned a final site suitability score (see Table 4.8). A ranked list of all ground-truthed sites was created from their final site suitability scores (Tables 4.10,4.11,4.12 & 4.14). These rankings identified sites most likely to be suitable for the establishment of BTRW colonies.
Any available comments and observations pertaining to shortlisted sites which were not ground-truthed were reviewed (Table 4.13). A list of these sites and relevant notes was compiled.

Observations made from lookouts and/or roads and other sites that were groundtruthed were also noted (Table 4.13). Of the 46 sites recommended by experts as potential BTRW habitat, but not ground-truthed, 13 sites have been listed as potentially appropriate for BTRW colonies (Table 4.13). div.head: Ground-truthing short-listed sites for their suitability as locations for the establishment of new Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby colonies
div.p: Many of the sites shortlisted by experts were not ground-truthed due to limited access because of recent recent heavy rainfall across the study area (Table 4.9 & 4.13). This rainfall caused substantial delays and several safety and accessibility issues. A total of 19 sites in Victoria and the ACT were ground-truthed (Little River Gorge = 11, Gariwerd = 6 and ACT = 2) (Table 4.9,4.10,4.11,4.12 & 4.14).

When ground-truthing sites predicted by the model to have habitat highly suitable for BTRW, it was observed that on-ground conditions were not always as represented by the model. The model output is represented by multiple pixels that create a location on a map. Each site was created by tracing multiple polygons over the model output. Many of these locations were sheer cliff faces, meaning that they were both inaccessible and did not include the appropriate attributes needed for BTRW occupancy. Ground-truthing for some sites showed that habitat just within/just outside the model output boundary identified more appropriate BTRW habitat.

div.head: Borderline sites
div.p: Of the 19 sites ground-truthed, four sites were considered borderline (Tables 4.10,4.11,4.12 & 4.14). Whilst many of these sites contained suitable rock, they were not considered complex enough to support a sustainable BTRW colony (Table 4.10,4.11 & 4.12). Little River Gorge site 44 and Gariwerd site 3 were easily accessed (Table 4.10, 4.11 & 4.12), which could result in higher predator prevalence rates.

div.head: Not suitable sites
div.p: Seven of the 19 ground-truthed sites were considered not suitable for BTRW (Tables 4.10,4.11 & 4.12). Many of these sites did not contain enough suitable rock complexity, required to support a sustainable BTRW colony (Table 4.10,4.11 & 4.12).

div.head: Victoria
div.p: Of the Victorian sites recommended by BTRW experts, but not ground-truthed, several are recommended for further investigation. Observations made from Little River Gorge complex site 121, found sites 114 and 115 appear to contain good BTRW habitat. Access to these sites is only possible via boat (Table 4.13). Sites assessed and deemed appropriate by previous studies include Little River Gorge complex site 112. These sites (112, 114 and 115) should be revisited and assessed against the criteria used in this study.

In conclusion, this study contributes to existing knowledge and literature and has filled significant gaps in the knowledge of site selection in BTRW translocations in both Victoria and the ACT. These results are extremely promising and will be used by the SBTRW Recovery Team to inform future BTRW translocations.

div.p: • Site access is extremely difficult • Site can be accessed partly via a walking track, but does require off track walking • Off-track walking requires navigation through heavily vegetated, rocky areas and the path to the site is not a clear and direct • The terrain is very steep and requires navigation over and through, gullies, rocks and through heavily vegetated areas • Access to site will take a long time

div.head: QUADRAT specific observations Site suitability for BTRW
div.p: • Within each site 3 polygons will be identified • The extent of each site is variable -polygons within the site will also vary
• Assessors can select a representative quadrat within the polygon to assess.

• Assessment will roughly be a 50m x 50m quadrat • Assessing these polygons within the site, will hopefully get a snapshot of the whole site and general area. • The comment section will allow for other information regarding both the attributes within the identified quadrats, but also for the areas outside that quadrat -see my filled-out assessment sheet examples Structural attributes for BTRW occupancy Based on rock complexity required for BTRW occupancy, assessors will be required to both comment and assess if each structural attributes are within each quadrat.

div.head: Rock complexity suitable for BTRW occupancy
div.p: Based on rock complexity required for BTRW occupancy, assessors will be required to both comment and rank each quadrat within the general site area.

div.head: Poor:
div.p: • Rock complexity is very poor • There is little to no caves, boulders, ledges, and overhangs • Site cannot be defended from predation Little:
• There is little to no rock complexity • There is little presences of caves, boulders, ledges, and overhangs • Site cannot be easily defended from predation

div.head: Good:
div.p: • There is moderate rock complexity • There is presences of caves, boulders, ledges, and overhangs • There are multiple entrances to caves and potential denning sites • There are boulder piles, that create habitat complexity • Site can be defended from predation, but there is still the opportunity for predation

div.head: Excellent:
div.p: • There is excellent rock complexity both within the quadrat, but also withing the surround areas • There is a high presence of caves, boulders, ledges, and overhangs • There are multiple entrances to caves, which will provide denning sites • There are boulder piles, which create habitat complexity, basking sites, and refuge from predation • Site can be easily defended from predation, through habitat complexity and multiple places for refugia

div.head: Exceptional:
div.p: • There is exceptional rock complexity both within the quadrat, but also withing the surround areas • There is a very high presence of caves, boulders, ledges, and overhangs • There are many entrances to caves, which will provide denning sites • There are many boulder piles, which create habitat complexity, basking sites, and refuge from predation • Site is easily defended from predation, through habitat complexity and multiple places for refugia
